item.title: Ask HN: What in the world is taking Ubuntu so long?
item.description: 179 points, 114 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article

→ HN comments  ·  179 points  ·  114 comments

Top #1 — throw0101c:

As outlined in this weblog post:

* https://ubuntu.com/blog/fixes-available-in-proposed-pocket-f...

The fixes were in the "proposed" repo since October 26 (noble) and 28 (resolute):

* https://launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux

One could pull them down at any point in the last week. Yesterday afternoon they were still in "proposed", but I checked this morning (EST/UTC-5) and they there were in "updates". Some tracking of timeline of when the updates to the repos happened seems to be available at:

* https://ma.ttias.be/linux-cve-2026-98432-vulnerable-kernels/

The kernels goes through an QA testing processes, and per this September post, they're looking at shortening the timeframe for kernel updates:

* https://canonical.com/blog/accelerating-delivery-of-cve-fixe...

↳ reply — gwbas1c:

> The kernels goes through an QA testing processes, and per this September post, they're looking at shortening the timeframe for kernel updates:

Looks like they aren't flexible enough to get a 4-line fix out the door when they need to.

These situations need a CEO or other high up to pull some people into a room, and basically say, "this needs to be released by EOD."

↳↳ reply — throw0101c:

> Looks like they aren't flexible enough to get a 4-line fix out the door when they need to.

Perhaps because Ubuntu, like most distros, release new kernels that include fixes and updates for more than one issue:

* https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2026:93413

* https://launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux/6.8.0-149.149

* https://www.suse.com/support/update/announcement/2026/suse-s...

* https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/DSA-6568-1

↳↳↳ reply — cassianoleal:

Perhaps that's the problem? Surely they use a version control system that allows them to branch off of older commit for these kinds of urgent patches.

Top #2 — imjonse:

Has there been a documented exploit of this CVE on Ubuntu or on the other distros before they were patched?

↳ reply 1 — talon8635:

Here’s the real answer. It’s not as scary as the original reporters made it out to be.

↳ reply 2 — arto:

See here: https://x.com/mattiasgeniar/status/2118040483154755627

Top #3 — atestu:

Seems like a good time to ask: what do people use, if not ubuntu, on a web server? Like for example for a rails app, on EC2... asking for a friend (who is me).

↳ reply 1 — kccqzy:

In the age of AI, there are only more and more security vulnerabilities to be discovered, and backporting all of them to outdated kernels will be nigh impossible. I’d not rather make such security patches dependent on the timeliness of backports especially if it is done by a distro rather than upstream. I suggest you use a rolling distro rather than anything with LTS kernels. The CVE in the original post CVE-2026-98432 is fixed since 7.3. If a distro doesn’t offer kernel 7.3.1 today, rule it out. (7.3.3 is also out today.)

In general I find distros using old kernels annoying because Linus treats compatibility seriously and “don’t break use space” has been a mantra for many years. On desktops in particular, GPU driver improvements like https://www.phoronix.com/news/Linux-7.3-DRM make it super worthwhile.

As for exactly which distro, it matters less than you think. I use openSUSE Tumbleweed but plenty of my friends prefer Arch.

↳↳ reply — SahAssar:

That is a wild take, especially consider the GP asked for a server use-case. Do you just assume that all new versions should be taken as soon as possible for all packages?

There is a balance: too outdated is bad, too eager for new versions is bad. The tradeoff that LTS tries to take is older, proven versions but with relevant security fixes quickly.

↳ reply 2 — mad182:

I personally use Debian both on my servers and desktops, for the last 15 years or so.

item.title: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk
item.description: 128 points, 58 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (cbc.ca)

→ HN comments  ·  128 points  ·  58 comments

Top #1 — Bender:

LLM bots are the easiest to spot. Rate limit them to 16kb/s and 1 request every 5 seconds. Give them a friendly multilingual WCAG status 429 page that says to slow down or status 444 and drop them into nftables ipsets if they continue to be aggressive. Ask your favorite LLM how to set this up. If your LLM gets session paused, ask Gemini or Grok. Tell it if you are behind a CDN. Enable logging of ssl curves, ciphers, etc... Show your LLM some examples from your access logs.

↳ reply 1 — eatonphil:

I get tens of thousands of IPs making 1 or 2 requests against pages on The Consensus (job search, code viewing, etc.). They're not super expensive pages. But I don't want to deal with the bot traffic (mostly because it messes up view counts I use to sell sponsorships). But then if I require an account (even a free one), valid readership is also going to drop with the new friction.

I could build something more complex to discover the patterns, or use Turnstile maybe. I'm not really sure at the moment.

↳↳ reply — EvanAnderson:

I mind a public access website for a government entity and this is exactly the pattern I see. US residential IPs make a couple of requests then never come back.

The bots may have layer 7 signatures that make them "easy" to block, but I'm dealing with COTS software with no ability to make changes to the stack. Even if I could by the time they're blocked the work is done and they're never coming back anyway.

I don't think I'm seeing the LLM bots in the scraping on this particular site. This site's data is highly sought-after by data brokers, legal services advertising, debt collectors, etc. I tend to think I'm seeing homespun scrapers. This site has been up for 20+ years and the scrapers seem to be well-adapted to using the HTML as an ad-hoc API for the data. The difference in the last few years has been the availability of vast numbers of residential proxies to mask the traffic.

↳ reply 2 — dmtroyer:

I think you overestimate many organizations ability to implement this type of rate-limiting.

Top #2 — blakesterz:

What I still don't understand is who is doing it? I assume it's not the big companies like OpenAI or Google or Anthropic, right? So there are a bunch of small things out there doing the scraping and then they sell it to the big places? Or are these just smaller AI models doing the scraping and using it for themselves? Is there an underground ecosystem where people buy and sell this stuff? I understand why it's valuable to the AI companies I'm curious about how all this work, the economics of it all.

↳ reply 1 — qingcharles:

Can't speak for everyone. I'm very gently scraping a lot of libraries for public domain periodical scans. The scans often exist nowhere else, or not in the same quality. Sometimes I find a certain library has perhaps the only known remaining intact copy of a periodical or a specific page.

The problem with the libraries is that all these scans are behind walls, so while the texts are public domain nobody can easily access them. I'm trying to liberate them and re-upload them outside the walls.

Until recently a lot of libraries would allow you to remotely sign up for a library card, but in the last 12 months almost all of them have reverted to having to bring ID in person to the library to validate your account, which puts the brakes on things.

↳↳ reply — sriacha:

I've been looking at historic newspapers recently, its bothersome and unfortunate that many (most?) are all behind newspapers.com (ancestry) paywall.

↳↳↳ reply — qingcharles:

Yeah, I'll be on ancestry.com and it says "We found this article about your great-grandfather!" and then you click it and it's newspapers.com and I have to close the tab.

What's the solution, though? All these newspapers won't scan themselves. I'm setting up a non-profit right now to deal with the magazines. The rights issues are both better and worse with magazines. "Better" in that most magazines have gone out of business and the rights are cheap. Worse in that most of them are orphans and the rights are very hard to track down.

↳ reply 2 — TazeTSchnitzel:

We're currently in the middle of an AI goldrush. There are probably hundreds of companies trying to do model pretraining. Anthropic and OpenAI and so on probably care about optics and implementing their crawlers properly. But there will be many firms few of us have heard of. I would guess some of them are Chinese, for example.

Top #3 — londons_explore:

Behind nearly every AI bot is some human who will see real benefit from scraping my site.

I just make sure all my pages are super lightweight to cache and serve from cloudflare and let the bots do what they like.

If I put something on the internet for all to see, I want bots to be able to see it too.

I've been on the other side of bot blocks - when I ask my LLM to buy me X and it comes back and says the only place it could buy from is some Bulgarian seller because everywhere else has anti-bot scripts, I make sure to give that Bulgarian site my business.

item.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
item.description: 629 points, 1388 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nbcnews.com)

→ HN comments  ·  629 points  ·  1388 comments

Top #1 — brightball:

After Helene knocked out power in parts of my area for a little over 14 days, I found out that a friend of ours used his cybertruck to power his house through the entire mess. He'd run the house on it for a couple of days, then drive the cybertruck over to a super charger station, recharge, then come home and plug the house back in.

The battery capacity on those things is equivalent to 9 Tesla Powerwall units or something close to it.

They may be ugly, but the emergency prepper in me always wanted one after hearing that story. Before, I always wanted to install powerwalls...but I never considered in an extended event being able to drive my powerwalls somewhere to recharge them.

↳ reply 1 — rurp:

This seems like an awfully niche case, no? How often does someone lose power at home for days, while also having a nearby and accessible charging station that stays functional the whole time? Most of the disasters I'm aware of people either get their power back in a short enough amount of time that they can use a normal generator for the gap, or things are bad and widespread enough that they aren't driving down the street to recharge their vehicle.

↳↳ reply — masklinn:

Also very important: the cybertruck is not the only vehicle capable of doing that (the keywords are V2H and V2L, V2H is the more convenient — the car just plugs into the mains and acts as a house battery — while V2L means you have to go and plug your stuff to the car's mains outputs directly)

> Most of the disasters I'm aware of people either get their power back in a short enough amount of time that they can use a normal generator for the gap

TBF an EV car has an absolutely massive battery relative to the electric consumption of a house, unless you're using resistive heating all around. Especially if you ration use.

↳↳↳ reply — jayknight:

Here's Alex from Technology Connections testing powering things in his house from his Hyundai Ioniq 5.

https://youtu.be/yO5fJ8z66Z8

↳ reply 2 — spaceywilly:

Another way to view this is that driving a cybertruck every day is quite wasteful (no different than driving a full size gas pickup every day). One recharge cycle in a cybertruck uses enough energy to power a typical home for 8 days, 130kWh. If you aren’t doing truck things with it, it’s better to drive a more efficient EV or hybrid car. It uses almost twice as much Wh per mile compared to a model Y.

I think this is why these EV trucks don’t do well (ford also cancelled the F150 lightning). For truck things, they aren’t particularly capable (you’d get less than 100 miles towing). For daily driving duty, a car or small suv is much more efficient. You can power your home during a storm from most EVs these days, you’d just have to top it up more often

↳ reply 3 — lrobinovitch:

This is now a feature of most new Tesla vehicles:

https://www.tesla.com/powershare/#vehicles

> Powershare allows you to draw power directly from your compatible Tesla vehicle to power your devices, your home or the grid.

> Powershare is currently available for all Cybertruck vehicles, and all new Model 3 and Model Y2 vehicles ordered on October 1, 2026 or later.

> To verify if your vehicle has Powershare, navigate to ‘Software’ > ‘Additional Vehicle Info’ > ‘Powershare Support: Enabled’ on your vehicle touchscreen.

Top #2 — crawshaw:

There are a lot of lenses through which to view the failure of the cybertruck: aesthetics, not enough truck not enough SUV, size, association of aesthetics with politics, etc. But I think the main one that is ignored is price.

The cybertruck was built in an era of high truck prices driven by zero interest rates. It bet on the price of trucks going up, just as the Ford F150 electric did. That was the wrong bet.

If it was a $40,000 truck, it would have a much bigger market despite all the other explanations of its failure. The market moved under it.

↳ reply 1 — gffrd:

The average price paid for a full-size truck in the US is north of $65,000.

- https://www.theautopian.com/the-average-full-size-truck-now-...

- https://www.ceicdata.com/en/united-states/new-vehicle-averag...

↳↳ reply — crawshaw:

And there has been 31% cumulative inflation since the cybertruck launched, so perhaps I should have said if it had been a $49,000 truck. But either way, it’s clearly a luxury vehicle that was disproportionately affected by interest rates.

↳↳↳ reply — jawilson2:

> it’s clearly a luxury vehicle that was disproportionately affected by interest rates

It's an electric vehicle sold by a racist, fascist, trillionaire Trump supporter. The Venn diagram of people who want an electric vehicle and who want to give Musk even more money is vanishingly small. My next vehicle will be an electric SUV, and I'm never touching a Tesla.

↳ reply 2 — al_borland:

I think another big one was the time from announcement to release.

When it was announced, for those who wanted an electric truck, it was going to be the only game in town. By the time Tesla delivered, there were several options already on the road from various companies. The people who really wanted an electric truck were already happy customers of another company by the time the cybertruck shipped. I see a fair number of Rivian, F-150 Lightning, and Hummer EVs around me.

When it comes to price, I expect to see a lot of Slate trucks once it starts shipping, with its low price.

Top #3 — paxy:

- Federal EV tax credits are over.

- The emissions credit market (where Tesla made most of its money) is dead due to lowered standards.

- Manufacturing costs haven't come down.

- EV sales share in the US is down to 6% (and falling every quarter).

- Chinese EVs are dominating every market outside the US.

- All the overhyped moonshots (sub-$30K car, unsupervised autopilot, autonomous robots) are nowhere to be seen.

It's hard to see where Tesla goes from here as a company. The stock is still surviving on Elon hype but has been stagnant for 5 years. The day he gets bored and decides to resign to focus on SpaceX full time the company is basically done.

↳ reply 1 — epistasis:

> EV sales share in the US is down to 6% (and falling every quarter).

It's not every quarter, but it's steady and that spells absolute disaster for US car manufacturers:

https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights/q3-2026-ev-sales-report-...

US car companies have been protected and bailed out too many times and are now not only completely uncompetitive on the global market, but set up to be completely demolished as EVs take over.

Their bad leadership and overall inefficiency mean that either investors are going to pay a massive price, or US consumers are going to pay a massive price. If we keep on pushing up consumer costs by propping up bad manufacturers with protectionism and bail outs, the US's entire economy is drug down by that.

There needs to be some creative destruction, ruthless culling of the least efficient manufacturers, so that their best workers can go to the better manufacturers, if the US is ever going to be a top tier car manufacturer again.

I hadn't followed just how bad US manufacturers were failing at EVs the past two years, what with all the other disasters unfolding, thanks for the wake up call. Two years of wasted time, of the US falling even farther behind... such a massive fail and yet not the most massive.

↳↳ reply — lesuorac:

> Two years of wasted time

Try two generations. I think it was obvious since the oil shocks that fossil fuels were not a good bedrock of the economy.

↳↳↳ reply — pjc50:

It's interesting to try to work out what the civ-style "dependency tree" of viable electric cars has been. It requires at the bare minimum high energy density light batteries, which were a spinoff of the cellphone revolution. As well as high efficiency digital power control, which while not impossible in 1970 would have been larger and heavier without modern SiC semiconductors.

Solar panels are an even more remarkable example of compounding a thousand different 1% improvements.

↳ reply 2 — scottyah:

- When it released, people were lighting Tesla stores and charging stations on fire, flipping off drivers, spitting on the cars even when kids were inside, and defacing them. This was generally supported, and for some reason a lot of people sided with the vandals in an effort to still be considered a Democrat and show hatred of The Other Side.

↳ reply 2 — amelius:

Hmm, after 5 minutes of browsing I still don't get it.

↳ reply 3 — cfontes:

Top #2 — 0x70dd:

↳ reply 1 — notfried:

A million monthly active users, even free ones, would cost you ~$10K/month on LaunchDarkly. A million sounds like a lot, but "active" can mean one visit, even anonymous users. ~$120K/year for feature flags is a ridiculous line item.

These SaaS companies are only valued this much because they charge based on MAUs, not request-based. I prefer PostHog's model. 100M requests/month is ~$2K [*].

[*] I'm not affiliated with PostHog.

↳↳ reply — ivarconr:

On Unleash Cloud: 100M request per month on Unleash cloud would be $235 + 75$ per seat ($53 Million requests included).

↳ reply 2 — vouwfietsman:

Shoutout to ConfigCat, https://configcat.com/

Same features as all these big guys, EU hosted, and down-to-earth pricing. Even the free tier got me quite far.

I'm unaffiliated btw.

Top #3 — jonhohle:

Are most feature flag systems really just simple Boolean checks like this with no feedback loop? In 2009 Amazon’s equivalent supported multi-variate flags (run test with more than 2 options), a feedback loop for performance/attribution, and weighting. I don’t see any of that on the unleash home page, but also haven’t seen it in other feature config systems either.

↳ reply — hobofan:

What you are describing is usually part of analytics platforms (Mixpanel, etc.). A feature flag toggle only plays a small part in this (but it may also be used for a lot of other scenarios of how you may want to control feature flags).

Audience is decided by analytics tool -> Feature flag server maps audience to feature flag value -> Analytics tool tracks its events and includes feature flag value as attribute

↳↳ reply — jonhohle:

So if you want to slowly roll out a feature flag, you need to get a different app involved that can do everything the feature flag tool can do and a whole lot more? What’s the point of the feature flag tool?

Analytics is a much broader set of tooling. It can (and should) report similar things.

↳↳↳ reply — hobofan:

The point of the feature flag tool is to control feature flags. They are not just for A/B testing and slow rollouts, and most products are not on the scale of Amazon, where you need to have a feedback loop for the rollout. Of course there is always going to be some overlap between tools, where many analytics platform allow you to do the rudimentary version of this.

The main point of a FF system is that you have a runtime-controllable mapping from user attributes to feature flags, where a set of logic rules can dictate who is exposed to what feature. With most analytics-tool based rollouts, you would be able to only directly set an attribute and you then hard-wire that attribute to the feature toggle in app code, which gives you a lot less flexibility and always requires a engineer in the hot path when it comes to doing rollouts.

Top #3 — stef25:

In Holland, GrapheneOS users are being targeted by police after "busting" a re-seller. The owners of the phones got raided without them being involved in any investigation. Just having the phone was enough to get a knock.

Supposedly the Dutch police had "cracked" their phones.

In Dutch https://archive.is/3wawb

↳ reply 1 — microtonal:

You fell for really shoddy reporting by AD/HLN:

According to our information, the reseller did not distribute official GrapheneOS. Using AI tools, he had built his own fork and added mobile device management (MDM) for remote administration. The result was a separate operating system that lacked, among other things, the security updates of the original project.

His signing keys for that system were probably compromised. Anyone holding those keys can build an update that the phones accept as genuine. Such an update was apparently installed on seized phones via ADB (Android Debug Bridge), an interface that requires a USB cable connection, and probably removed the screen lock. The phones could then be examined forensically. On our information, the authorities again needed the phone in their hands. On official GrapheneOS, the same approach would require the project's own signing keys.

https://www.joint-defense-team.com/post/grapheneos-cracked-p...

↳↳ reply — ledoge:

I don't think the attack can work as described here. One of the features that GrapheneOS lists is:

> Insider attack resistance for updates to the secure element (Owner user authentication required before updates are accepted)

From my understanding, this means that even if you do have the signing keys, you cannot install an update that would remove the need for knowing the screen lock to unlock the filesystem's encryption - as installing such an update requires entering the screen lock first.

↳↳↳ reply — buzer:

However if you have signing keys and access to the update delivery infra you could just publish the update and wait for it to get auto updated before starting to seize the phones.

↳ reply 2 — 3abiton:

This is the issue with being lenient on crime but also being liberal. You have to search for the "right" patterns to find your criminal. It happens that folks who care about privacy, and criminals, two distinct groups search and use the same set of technologies: wether it's grapheneOS, or others. I am also tired of people still looking suspicious at me for not having instagram, snap or tiktok or use whatsapp, it's like I dropped out of society, and that I use linux and use open source email clients/server, I use ublock origin advanced with blocking of scripts and 3rd party domains. Why privacy is an uphill daily battle.

(Reposts are fine after a year or so; links to past threads are just to satisfy extra-curious readers)

Top #2 — mturmon:

Peter makes some excellent points in TFA and it’s a fun read.

But the situation has moved on, moving even further beyond the assertions Peter makes about the utility of the black-box generative approach.

In particular, LLMs are telling us a lot about those low-probability, never before seen sentences — it’s called CALU, the creative aspects of language use.

LLMs exhibit CALU; as we know they will happily create such sentences. And inspecting the LLMs does provide insight:

“It does change the epistemic situation substantially. A working system can be inspected, perturbed, retrained, lesioned, and compared with other systems. Building is not understanding, but it gives understanding a strong foothold.

Explaining creative language use in LLMs would not, by itself, explain creative language use in humans. But the artificial case matters even if the mechanisms turn out to be substantially different. At a minimum, LLMs are an existence proof of one pathway by which open-ended, context-sensitive language can arise.”

For much more, see this substack by Chandra Sripada, a U of Michigan linguist:

https://chandrasripada.substack.com/p/ai-and-the-retreat-of-...

He is interviewed by Sean Carroll on his excellent Mindscape podcast:

https://preposterousuniverse.com/podcast/2026/08/10/363-chan...

Top #3 — crtified:

No empirical fact is restricted to a singular vector through human language.

"..if we think of truth as something of granite-like solidity and of personality as something of rainbow-like intangibility and reflect that the aim of [human writing] is to weld these two into one seamless whole, we shall admit that the problem is a stiff one and that we need not wonder if [human writers], for the most part failed to solve it." - Virginia Woolf

[human writing, human writers] = [biography, biographers] in the original quote. My edit is because I infer that her statements key point is that of the biological subjectivity inherent to all human prose.

item.title: Britain to make salary disclosure in job ads mandatory
item.description: 532 points, 414 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (reuters.com)

→ HN comments  ·  532 points  ·  414 comments

Top #1 — dotdi:

I will repost a comment I made here a while ago on a similar discussion. Salary non-disclosure is a dealbreaker for me since being through the situation described below:

A few years back I wanted to get out of the work situation I was in. I looked around, had some interviews, had some offers. None of the postings had salary ranges, as is common where I live.

My eyes, however, were set on a specific small company because I liked their product. The process was long and involved multiple meetings, a take-home problem, and stretched over 2 or so months. I was upfront about what my salary expectations were (wasn't looking for a raise, just a lateral move). They said we discuss salary when you meet the founders, i.e. the last step before getting hired, but they also didn't tell me that my range was way off.

Turns out I had played this 9 week game and turned down other offers just to be severely low-balled by them. Maybe they saw that I really wanted the position and thought they could get away with a low offer.

Obviously, I rejected their offer on the spot. I also promised myself to never, _ever_, be fooled like that again. We talk money before I invest any significant amount of time or I walk.

EDIT: fixed wording.

↳ reply 1 — cs02rm0:

I've done worse than that. I've taken the job on a lower salary, being told I'd get a promotion and pay rise in 6 months. That didn't happen. And then when it didn't happen at 18 months they dangled the carrot of a promotion up two levels. After a few weeks of not hearing about it I popped a resignation letter in the post one morning, went into the office and had an email to say the promotion had "gone away".

Then they went legal trying to prevent me working for a competitor.

I actually got what I needed from the role anyway, but it was a lesson to heed the red flags. I've not heeded that lesson a couple of times recently, just because the market seems to be toast, but it's not been worth it.

↳ reply 2 — DeusExMachina:

A friend that works as a manager told me that companies stretch the interview process on purpose so that at the end you will accept a lower offer that you normally would because you are exhausted by the process.

↳ reply 3 — kevin_thibedeau:

> small company

> Stretched over two months

These companies aren't Google. There is no valid reason why it should take so long to decide on candidates for a position. It is not necessary to have more than two interview sessions. I bail on any company that subjects people to this garbage.

Top #2 — aregue:

I have always felt that job ads should include salary information. The main reason is not to waste anyone's time. Often a narrow salary range or a clear link between requirements and salary are much more informative than a job description. I have experienced to apply to a job opening and go through one or more interviews only to find out that the company is actually hiring for a more junior position than the ad copy implied.

A second reason is to avoid discrimination. Applicants that feel disadvantaged, even if they are actually qualified, may hesitate to negotiate for a higher salary in the same way that a other applicants would. The consequence is that they start with a lower salary. This applies specially to women. Plenty of research shows that they are less likely to negotiate their salary.

Research[1] suggests that pay transparency leads to lower average salaries because employers avoid paying higher wages to any one employee to avoid costly negotiations with others. The effect is small, around 2%, and it disappears with increasing degree of unionization. In my opinion this is an acceptable price to pay to reduce pay inequality, which often is much more than 2%. It is also a good argument for joining a union.

[1] https://www.nber.org/papers/w28903

↳ reply 1 — arpinum:

When hiring I don't have a narrow range in mind, it can be 50% or more. I look at the individual and make a judgment call on their impact to the business. For software we don't have a widget factory where employees are easily substitutable.

I've tried the opposite, paid everyone the same. But there were clear differences in ability and more importantly outside options. It became a problem when it came to retention and the business didn't have the ability to overpay everyone to keep the top performers.

↳↳ reply — chaosharmonic:

You're describing levels. If your range is so wide the top of the range is double the bottom of the range, you're hiring at multiple levels, and you should just say that. You should also have more detailed descriptions that help you and candidates differentiate what those levels are.

More broadly than that -- it's not that you need to pay everyone the same, it's that you need clear structure around how your pay works.

An example that became a problem with one previous employer was that they kept saying "performance" was their only determining factor for pay, after it had come out that exactly one person on our team had been offered bonuses as a performance incentive.

It's not actually performance-based if you have different and better reward structures, or if you can't/won't explain why gaps exist.

↳↳↳ reply — arpinum:

It's mainly specialties, not just levels. Are you a graphic designer that can also build your designs for the web? Were you previously consulting for our largest customer? Do you speak Welsh for our important client in Pembroke? Did you previously work in tech stack X and want to get back to it, and could lead our effort into that market? I'll pay more for these even if they come in at the same grade. Pay is very subjective, it is a prediction about the value an employee can or does bring balanced against their next best option.

↳ reply 2 — lelanthran:

I've always asked, and then get the generic "for the ideal candidate we are prepared to go very high", which I tactfully point out as the BS it is - there is no role that has ever been advertised without a manager or director-level sign-off on the range.

I usually reply to the brush-off with "I only ask because the seniority level is reflected in the salary, not the role or the advertisement."

I say that because it is, in fact, true: the seniority/skill required for the role and duties/responsibilities dictates the pay, the bullet points in the advertisement and the role description is often completely divorced from the level of seniority or skill required in the actual role.

IOW "We're hiring a Senior dev" might have me respond "That's a Junior pay-bracket".

Top #3 — ellen364:

Cautiously pleased about this. Some companies in UK pay senior devs £30-35k. And some companies won't discuss that until v late in the process, while importing US-style multiround interviews. It's pretty silly when people get 3 rounds in, take time off work for the interviews, then find out their expectations are so far apart.

↳ reply 1 — illwrks:

Advice for anyone in future.

Recruiters at big companies will be told to advertise the role within the payband (the min to max pay for that role at that pay band)

So if you see a top end number and think you’ll get that, you probably won’t it will be around the middle of the range.

At that point you go back to the recruiter and state that you would expect the top end of the range. They may agree with you but then keep in mind that may also impact your salary increase at the end of the year, meaning a smaller increase for you compared to your peers which over several years would even out and out you back in the middle of the payband like your peers. This is why the common idea is to jump roles every few years.

↳ reply 2 — steve_adams_86:

Huh, I thought I was paid on the lower end for my field. Well, I suppose I still am (working for a NGO), but £30-35k is absurd. That's not reasonable for any skilled role, really. Why do people accept it? Are salaries for software in the UK generally very low? Even lower than Canada? I find it hard to believe, but then, I have no data to go off of.

The main way they can surprise you today is pulling in information that’s new TO YOU - I impressed with the algorithms they pop out sometimes simply because never formally studied compsci. But when it treads on my home turf I find it very basic, and for bigger picture stuff like system architecture its terrible, by its nature it doesn’t have a “vision” of how the whole system fits together

↳ reply 1 — z3t4:

It's like reading a news paper, when it's about your field of expertise you find lots of errors, but when it's about something you don't know you take it at face value.

↳↳ reply — layer8:

The short name for that is Gell-Mann amnesia.

↳ reply 2 — manapause:

Strong agree. My 30 years of experience building computers and breaking them has made me better because I don’t trust my knowledge or myself as a first principle. If I didn’t have that and I could easily see myself in an alternate reality, coming in late to the game to leverage ai to build a car out of seatbelts; harnessing all the power of 1000 suns seeing that idea to fruition.

↳ reply 3 — BenoitP:

Strong agree, but with a major caveat: First since we humans don't have a memory the size of the internet, new TO YOU is extremely easy to find. And second: a lot of discoveries can be made by trying to match two different domains and generate new insights at the seams.

A lot of math theorems are discovered that way by humans btw: find a difficult problem in a domain, map it to another domain, apply existing theorems there, go back to the original domain. The only difference is an LLM would have to search for an interesting problem, but that can be done by brute-forcing search at the seams and validating the problem does not previously exists. And there is no new TO YOU for the LLM: it can get help from a vast amount of helper domains.

IMHO there's a shot at having category theory really unifying a large chunk of maths in the next decade. It'll be a big ugly ball of Lean, but a queryable one at that.

Top #2 — nfw2:

I've also found it very hard to leave AI agents up to their own devices for long periods and get much productive benefit from it.

I suppose it's possible that frontier labs have internal models that are so far beyond that autonomous research becomes possible, but I'm not sure that's it.

It seems to me like these models are like a very competent, important part of some hypothetical digital brain, but alone they don't have all the facilities they need to be useful, like a genius with severe ADHD and short-term memory loss.

For anything where quality isn't objective in a clear-cut way, very intentional context management is needed to get good outputs. As context size expands, performance degrades. As the number of tasks increases, performance degrees. As the number of independent decisions based on subjective criteria increases, performance degrees.

If you can get a harness that makes sure every decision is made one at a time, focused with only the context it needs, things work great. But making those harnesses is still hard, a lot of work, and something that agents seem to have no clue how to help you with.

↳ reply — nathias:

I don't think its the frontier models, my opus 5.5 has no problem working on a project fairly autonomously, for example if I prompt it in the evening it will work the whole night without issues...

Top #3 — p1necone:

On one hand, yeah, I agree.

On the other hand, using AI to trawl through all the grunt work, experiments, and well trodden areas means I can crawl up pretty close to that giants shoulder and spend way less effort myself answering the actually important questions so I can stand on it.

(This isn't supposed to sound self aggrandising - the giants whose shoulders I'm standing on aren't very tall, and they probably have bigger brothers and sisters, but the idiom was too good of a match to pass up using)

↳ reply 1 — loveparade:

The thing is, without doing the grunt work you usually don't have enough understanding to answer the big questions.

Ask anyone who has an advanced degree in math or physics. They will tell you that doing the boring practice problems over and over is usually the key to understanding, not reading the high level theorems.

↳ reply 2 — Matumio:

The proper term is: "On the shoulders of a very large pyramid of hobbits." The concept is the very core of human intelligence, also known as cultural evolution. I can't resist to recommend Joseph Henrich's book "The Secret of Our Success" every few years here, to anyone interested in human intelligence, and how it is different from other primates.

There was a critical review article with a title that summarizes the book well: "On the shoulders of a very large pyramid of hobbits, or why we are not just very smart chimps. The Secret of Our Success: How Culture is Driving Human Evolution, Domesticating Our Species, and Making Us Smarter." Obviously I got triggered by your comment, which was eerily close to that title.

Top #1 — bargl:

I worked on modernization in the FAA specifically around digitizing NOTAMs.

I would urge you not to consider this modernization from the perspective you may be familiar, as someone who may work on the bleeding edge and sometimes sees a lack of caution from engineers pushing for change.

The FAAs safety risk management is built around a rigorous process, but that is also a massive slowdown to reasonable progress.

One of the eng I worked with was 80+ years old and just didnt want to retire. He did not understand modern systems at all and the risks we were looking at were not (imo) realistically balanced.

I get the idea that the current administration is pushing safety to the side, but there is another risk where safety becomes a blocker to reasonable change.

When I left that work (more than 15 years ago) it was clearly a blocker.

↳ reply 1 — kalcode:

This isn't like COBOL. Floppy disc were never reliable. They should've been phased out a long time ago

Magnetic degradation, wear from read/write heads, and environmental sensitivity mean disks have a natural expiration date and it's not long. And they are also easy to corrupt from all kinds of magnetic sources around us.

I get other stuff, even DOS like system. Safety critical software/hardware that was battle tested makes sense. Not floppy. Sometime it's just bureaucracy.

↳↳ reply — spullara:

my 1980s 5.25" disks still work. i'm surprised but they have laster a long time.

↳↳↳ reply — hermitdev:

3.5" floppies were still common while I was in college. I have distinct memories of copying a project to a floppy in my dorm room, popping the disk out, walking next door (literally next door in the dorms, not even going outside up or down stairs or anything), popping the disk into a team member's PC and the project being gone. We laughed it off and chucked the disk in the trash and got another. Project wasn't lost-lost since I had a copy on my hard disk. This was also the era of the 100MB Zip Drives, which I also had in my PC and thankfully all of our lab PCs had, too. That's what I normally used for all of my day-to-day file transfers of any real import. I still have my zip disks, but I seem to have lost my zip drive, so no idea if the disks still have any data on them.

↳ reply 2 — riazrizvi:

Within this is a further heartening reassurance that I chose a profession I will be able to do until my dying day. But at 55 I see my safest option is my own business where some higher up doesn't take me off a role I improve to give it to someone they know.

↳ reply 3 — andyjohnson0:

> One of the eng I worked with was 80+ years old and just didnt want to retire. He did not understand modern systems at all and the risks we were looking at were not (imo) realistically balanced.

Can you recall anything that that engineer said or did which turned out to be credible? Or which you perhaps learned from?

Top #2 — snvzz:

Replacing the drives with FlashFloppy would not be a crazy idea as a first step.

Top #3 — jonhohle:

More information needed. Was this a sneakernet? No one thought of replacing with a floppy emulator and SD cards? All of the data can fit into 1.44MB?

If the last one is true, devs take note. If FAA can rely on slow, small storage for safety critical applications, you probably can reduce the resource requirements for your app and improve your customers’ experience and extend the life of their hardware.

↳ reply — shermantanktop:

> devs take note

There’s been an incredible expansion of computer hardware and networking in every dimension since the heyday of the floppy. And the floppy itself was a huge step up from technology of even a few years prior.

Your comment could have been made in any year since 1950, and it would have been both correct and irrelevant outside the areas most resistant to hardware upgrades. FAA is conservative, and should be, but the rest of us have supercomputers in our pockets.

Have software developers abused the hardware capabilities they have been granted? Of course they have. I’d love to see some care put into that. But beyond the basics, hand-twiddled hyperoptimizations are now an exercise for craftspeople. Or…AI?

↳↳ reply — al_borland:

> but the rest of us have supercomputers in our pockets.

The issue is they don't feel like supercomputers, because of how much they've been taken for granted.

My computer and phone today feel no faster or better to use than they did 20 years ago. They might be vastly more capable for niche applications, but for the day-to-day stuff it seems like we keep buying new hardware, so we can run the latest software at the same old speeds, mostly for security updates.

I have an M1 MBP... a bit old, but still does everything I need. When I click Calendar in the dock (when it is already open, but just haven't used it in a while), it can take 3-5 seconds to come to the front as the active app. It feels broken. This wait wasn't a thing 5 years ago on this hardware, nor was it an issue on a PPC Mac from 25 years ago. Yet now its' a problem... why? So the UI can calculate the refraction of the background image in the liquid glass? Should I be spending $2,500 on a new MBP just to switch more quickly from my browser to the Calendar? It doesn't make much sense.

item.title: Claude Code sends your email address to websites
item.description: 1363 points, 433 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1363 points  ·  433 comments

Top #1 — varenc:

Many people report seeing this behavior when using the SEC API specifically which makes me think that service is requesting this. Maybe email is required by the SEC API?

---

UPDATE: The SEC API documentation requires your email in the User-Agent and will reject you otherwise. Demo:

    U='https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyconcept/CIK0000320193/us-gaap/Assets.json'
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  curl default User-Agent, rejected\n'  "$U"
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  email in user-agent, success\n' -A 'Acme Research admin@acme-research.example' "$U"

    response: 403  curl default, rejected
    response: 200  email in user-agent, success
SEC docs: https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/a...

So basically Claude is trying to problem solve, and just does what the SEC asks. It's a 'prompt injection attack', but the entity instructing this behavior is the SEC. Tricky alignment problem. Pretty silly mechanism, since of course there's no email validation. (edit: turns out the SEC will accept most any non-cURL user-agent, email not actually required)

↳ reply 1 — T-R:

I work with the SEC data, and have a work contact e-mail explicitly for this. I similarly caught Claude happily sending my personal e-mail (likely just the e-mail associated with the Claude account), without prompt or warning, only because I happened to catch it in the curl requests. Definitely a security concern that Claude generally has this behavior, even if in this specific instance it was more of a mild annoyance.

↳↳ reply — DANmode:

It’s a completion-machine.

Not an omniscient personal assistant.

They haven’t piled enough gates on top of that initial technological hole yet.

↳↳↳ reply — ZiiS:

Most human personal assistants are equally vulnerable to this prompt injection.

↳ reply 2 — devsda:

Will be interesting to see how 402 payment required will be treated.

What if someone spins up a web endpoint that returns 402 with instructions on how to pay like CC details in the headers etc, or may be an openapi spec to provide payment and get an auth token, when you have given the agent access to your password vault for authentication to other services.

↳ reply 3 — jessriedel:

It's not an alignment problem. The SEC can reject your request if it lacks an email address, but it can't order you to provide it here. So Claude should just not submit anything requiring the email address and come back to you with the reason things didn't work.

Top #2 — grey-area:

Biggest questions here, which I think need answering:

Should Claude have access to user details? I’d say no, unless explicitly entered manually into a chat.

Should Claude have access to anything outside of the sandboxed project files without explicit permission? I’d again say no.

Should Claude have internet access without a clear log of all requests made?

Instances of Claude should be heavily sandboxed and kept away from user data, far more so than they are now. The impression given by the desktop UI is that the LLM only has access to things explicitly added to a project.

This impression is not true, as evidenced by Claude pulling data from other sessions outside a project even when not instructed to (I’ve seen this a few times), and in this case pulling your email (from account details, user contacts? I wonder where it got that info?).

None of this information should be available to Claude, by design, not by instruction. Using text instructions to try to limit these machines is an incredibly flawed approach and should not be necessary for important info. Anthropic should have the model access completely locked down by controls at the os level over file access, not open by default. That is how to fix this.

If a user wants to open access that should be an explicit choice from them, with a warning about possible consequences.

↳ reply 1 — jstanley:

> Should Claude have access to user details?

This is hard to avoid. All it needs to do is make a git commit and look in the git log and it will find out who you are.

↳ reply 2 — wodenokoto:

> Should Claude have access to anything outside of the sandboxed project files without explicit permission? I’d again say no.

This is definitely a question that sounds straightforward but isn't. Like, when I ask antigravity to commit to git, it gets an error because ~/.gitconfig is outside the sandbox.

Top #3 — mk89:

This explains the amount of spam emails I am receiving in the work email since I switched to Claude. I used to work with copilot which was fine. Now I am getting really a lot of spam emails almost on a daily basis. Absolutely crazy. And they are even personalised with my name and surname, not just "dear customer"...

Stupid me, I thought they somehow had hacked my company database or so... (considering all the cves, attacks happening on a daily basis...).

↳ reply 1 — crazygringo:

It almost certainly does not explain it, and is probably just a coincidence.

Claude Code is not sending your email address to websites as a default, or regularly. It is not some automatic header or anything.

Rather, if you are performing certain kinds of research on sites that involves downloading certain kinds of information, like on Wikipedia or the SEC, it supplies your e-mail address when the sites request it as part of their download policy. As part of anti-bot policy. Obviously Claude should have asked for approval first, but Claude isn't out there just spamming your e-mail address in every external request it makes or anything.

Wikipedia and the SEC are not selling your e-mail address to spammers. And these are the two main sites where it has come up.

↳↳ reply — throwup238:

Yep it’s mainly happened to me when I was playing around with the EVE Online API via Claude. The game developer asks everyone to put their emails into the request headers so they can contact users to fix their buggy scripts and stuff.

↳ reply 2 — weird-eye-issue:

I highly doubt this is connected

Usually this is from LinkedIn, GitHub, etc scraping... There are databases where they just guess and verify emails too

item.title: $2.5T has been wiped from US stocks
item.description: 145 points, 130 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (finlaws.substack.com)

→ HN comments  ·  145 points  ·  130 comments

Top #1 — foolswisdom:

For all the federal election related takes, remember that

1. Market price changes are changes from what was expected before compared to what is expected now. And not even only in regards to the asset itself, but with respect to comparative change in other assets as well. 2. conventional wisdom when the branches of government are divided, less change comes from the government, so you can expect that your expectations for the future will remain stable, and that confidence reduces risk aversion, resulting in higher pricing.

Therefore, the market going down cannot be attributed purely to a question of who is in charge, because the democrats can't pass anything unless they get a nice number of Republicans on their (possible I suppose, but I don't think anyone is expecting that right now). But it could be attributed to expectations of what Republicans would do vs now that they can't.

Besides, it's basically impossible (or at least for layman, who knows if you're a market maker?) to accurately attribute a day's market behavior to any event, with a compelling causal explanation (sometimes your attribution could also be explained to have the opposite effect than the one you're trying to explain) and not ignoring alternate possible explanations.

It's kinda annoying when even otherwise serious people invoke the market movement of a day as an meaningful event that can be explained (notwithstanding that by tomorrow the effect might have reversed). But unfortunately business news like CNBC promotes that kind of thinking.

↳ reply 1 — foolswisdom:

It's still quite possible that all the non federal items on the ballot (lots of anti data center referendums, lots of democrat politicians in state office) matter quite a bit.

↳ reply 2 — yojo:

State government leadership did change in unexpected ways, and they do get to pass laws. See: Texas

↳ reply 3 — mgh2:

Wait for 40% downside: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HfcDQ7JVnzQ

Nvidia can be down to 3-3.5T market cap from 5-5.7T heights

Top #2 — schnuri:

I always find these market cap numbers misleading. The US stock market isn't "worth" $2.5T less. If you multiply the marginal share price by the total number of shares, you get a number that's $2.5T lower. That is something different. E.g., if you tried to sell all Nvidia shares at once, you'd never get anywhere near ~$4.5T (just as buying them all would cost far more).

↳ reply 1 — smallmancontrov:

> if you tried to sell all Nvidia shares at once

That is something different: liquidation value. Market cap tells you the sum total of the numbers next to this ticker symbol in everyone's brokerage account. It tells you the collective expectations about future returns and also the wealth effect that people feel based on their ability to individually obtain cash for shares.

It is true that neither of those things is liquidation value, but also liquidation value is neither of those things. If you expect a liquidation scenario, sure, use liquidation value. If you don't expect a liquidation scenario but want to measure collective expectations of and confidence in a stock, use market cap.

↳↳ reply — jwpapi:

but it’s still so wrong. Like if I fund a company and I sell 1% to my mum who really believes in me for 100.000 USD I’m suddenly worth almost 10 million and the market cap of my company is 10 million, even though nobody might even pay a penny for my company. I don’t think most people are aware that this is how it works and crypto currencies have abused this a lot, by just selling a part of their shares, creating scarcity in the market and reaching high market caps. The traditional financial market is not that much different I feel like.

If Elon Musks sells all his shares the value of SpaceX and Tesla would drop dramatically I don’t know how much realistically he would be able to liquidate from his shares.

So the headline "is wiped" is misleading. I think it’s all ultimatively to get money in the markets and support growth

↳ reply 2 — adam_arthur:

What something's worth is what somebody is willing to pay for it.

And conventionally, we use the marginal buyer's bid as the measuring stick for public companies. e.g. the share price

Of course, the intrinsic value based on currently known data/fundamentals is unchanged.

But many market valuations are disconnected from that to begin with. Loans, options, warrants, many things are tied to the market cap/share price of a company. E.g. what is the LTV ratio when lending? What are my RSUs worth?

Top #3 — curiousllama:

This is definitely scary, but not the end of the world (yet).

The S&P500 is still up ~7% YTD, and 5y CAGR of 9.4% before dividends, in line with historical norms.

This is primarily a decline in tech: week over week, the S&P is -4.5% (SPX), but the S&P excluding tech is +0.1% (SPXT).

Right now, this looks like speculation that tech will reduce capex after Q4 earnings (Nvidia, Micron, Sandisk, AMD all down >2x vs the S&P). But it'll take time to tell; most just announced Q3 a week ago.

All this to say: expect volatility, but no need to panic.*

*(Unless you're in TQQQ. Then panic.)

In case anyone else was wondering:

TQQQ is the only ETF (Exchange-traded Fund) that targets 3x the daily returns of the Nasdaq-100 Index.

Ouch!

↳ reply 2 — staticman2:

It's not scary at all unless you think stocks are a riskless asset expected to always go up and bonds and bank accounts are for suckers.

item.title: Goodbye from Salon
item.description: 537 points, 195 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (salon.com)

Top #1 — legitster:

The amount of newsroom jobs fell 60% between 2008 and 2020. The vast majority of what was lost were "beat" reporters - foreign bureaus, Washington bureaus from regional publications, statehouse reporters, or regional specialty beats (science, law, etc).

This started long before the decline of the open internet and AI. If anything, the shift online covered up a massive hollowing out of the industry. We're getting fewer sources of news, and more national coverage. A lot of stuff that is reported on is coming from a scant number of wire services, or directly from PR teams themselves.

For the most part, your choice of news platform is just a layer of coverage choices and political spin on top of a very thin market of original coverage.

↳ reply 1 — mapontosevenths:

> The amount of newsroom jobs fell 60% between 2008 and 2020. [0]

That was a scary number so I Googled it. You should always check scary numbers. It's misleading.

It's true that newspaper newsroom jobs fell 57% (from roughly 71,000 to 31,000 jobs) over that period. However, newsroom employment across all mediums fell by only 26% (from 114,000 to 85,000).

A lot of hose jobs went digital, they didn't just disappear.

[0] https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2021/07/13/u-s-newsr...

↳↳ reply — jacobolus:

Your page has:

> Newspaper newsroom employment fell 57% between 2008 and 2020, from roughly 71,000 jobs to about 31,000. At the same time, the number of digital-native newsroom employees rose 144%, from 7,400 workers in 2008 to about 18,000 in 2020.

So, if we group digital publications with newspapers we are going from 78k to about 49k jobs, a drop of almost 40%. It would be interesting to see a finer grained breakdown by type of jobs. I would speculate that there was probably an even bigger decline in the number of journalists per se.

The rest of the numbers you are quoting are mostly broadcast TV, with some radio and cable TV folks thrown in. My impression is that quite few of those jobs / stories are serious journalism.

This was so topical for that time period that I assumed it had been written a few years earlier e.g. 2006. Turns out it was written in 1998!

→ Article (pangram.com)

→ HN comments  ·  132 points  ·  64 comments

Top #1 — sean_pedersen:

An ill advised undertaking IMO: Any attempt to build AI generated content detection systems is flawed, since the outputs of such a system may be used to train an even better fake data generator. This leads to an equilibrium state of digital uncertainty: nothing in the digital realm can be deemed as real anymore - only as digital.

↳ reply 1 — modeless:

AI detectors can't work in theory, but Pangram works well in practice. This is because the AI companies are not trying to fool Pangram. They have no incentive to; in fact the incentive goes the opposite way. They want to watermark their outputs to leave no doubt as to whether something was generated by their AI.

↳↳ reply — orbital-decay:

AI companies might have no incentive but determined actors do, by definition. Anything Pangram could possibly do (even semantic variation detection) can be trivially bypassed by doing img2img on a custom trained local model, which is in itself done trivially in practice by many people. Same for text, train it on anything and use distribution-aware sampling. From your words, you already have false sense of reliable detection, so a work of a determined actor will trick you into believing false negatives.

↳ reply 2 — bananaflag:

This is what I've been saying for years, then I was surprised by Pangram actually working.

Sometimes it pays to attempt the impossible.

↳ reply 3 — edude03:

This is how ai is trained anyway - generative adversarial networks

Top #2 — hex4def6:

At least on gemini generated images vs real ones, it works surprisingly well.

Taking a photo of an AI generated image on my grubby laptop screen with my phone, moire and all, still got detected. So the signal it's using is pretty robust.

An actual photo you took is not AI-generated though.

Where’s the line? If you take a selfie in Times Square, and there’s an AI-generated image in an ad behind you, that photo you took isn’t AI-generated.

item.title: Image of our satellite-choked night skies
item.description: 126 points, 100 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (kottke.org)

→ HN comments  ·  126 points  ·  100 comments

Top #1 — bradgessler:

A few things:

Satellites are only visible shortly after sunset and before sunrise, known as astronomical twilight.

If the images in the photograph upset you and you think our night sky is ruined, the thing that kills it the most is light pollution. Flood lights, parking lights, and street lights that don’t direct light down to the ground make viewing much worse than satellites for everybody.

It’s just as easy to capture incredible images of the night sky, even during astronomical twilight, with image processing. Here’s photos I’ve captured in my driveway in the SF Bay Area: https://bradgessler.github.io/observatory-blog/observations/

I captured said images with an Elixir software stack I installed on a Pi and hooked up to my telescope. It’s open-source at https://github.com/bradgessler/observatory for those who are interested. I hook Claude up to it and it runs observations for the night, processes images with deterministic tools, and publishes them as the night progresses.

↳ reply 1 — happytoexplain:

People on HN who are "upset", or believe (correctly, of course) that night sky observation/recording/appreciation is increasingly impeded over time, do not feel that way because of this image.

Yes, terrestrial light pollution has been the number one problem since we invented electric lights, but satellites and terrestrial light pollution are both separate problems with different effects and different coverage. E.g. even though light pollution is much more harmful, you can escape it with a short drive, even if you live in a densely populated region. You can't escape the strings of satellites.

Separately: "Shortly after sunset" is a downplay. It can be hours. But in any case, it's the time when the vast majority of stargazers are looking at the stars (with their eyes).

Satellites have the same awkward sociopolitical energy infecting them as all tech does nowadays. But remember: There is absolutely nothing wrong with being upset about the effect of these satellites, just like there is absolutely nothing wrong with being upset about the effect of electric lights. You can certainly get a lot of mileage out of weighing this against the consequences of having much fewer satellites, and that's exactly where all the argument should be occupied. That they affect the night sky, which reasonably annoys many people, is just a fact.

↳↳ reply — wtch98:

When I look at the night sky with my eyes I don't see the picture shown. I might see a few moving lights, sometimes they are planes, sometimes satellites. They're magical, just like a meteor or the space station, but they don't annoy me at all.

One of my most memorable night viewings was some years ago when I was in Cyprus, lovely and warm, sat looking overhead. I saw a bright light and a dark light perhaps 2 or 3 degrees (more than a thumb, less than 3 fingers) apart travelling at the same speed. I later found out it was a Dragon carbon ship detatched from the space station and on its way back to splashdown less than an hour later in the pacific.

↳ reply 2 — nuccy:

For naked eye observations definitely not a problem in comparison with light polution. Though for astronomers, especially those looking with sensitive instruments (SIPM and SPAD cameras) for transient events (like asteroid occultation or ultrafast photometery) all those satellites will create fake signals - about 1ms dips in the brightness now and then.

↳ reply 3 — lenkite:

Even if humanity becomes an inter-stellar civilization, we will still have satellites polluting the night-sky on any planet! They are an eternal fixture of our civilization now - as long as we don't go extinct.

Top #2 — jefftk:

A lot of people are going to look at that manually edited image, think it's a traditional long-exposure photo, and conclude that satellites are much more of a problem for astronomy than they really are.

The photographer made a really neat picture, but Kottke is presenting it with a headline that suggests its something else, and generally not giving enough context (mostly just blockquotes).

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

Ironically, the same technique used to remove the stars and isolate the satellites could have been used to remove the satellites and isolate the stars.

It would take 100X less effort to remove the satellites.

↳↳ reply — happytoexplain:

Why is that ironic?

You're just pointing out that there are tools to automate this.

↳↳↳ reply — Aurornis:

The photographer didn’t use automated tools. He edited it manually and said it took a very long time.

It’s ironic because stars outnumber visible satellites by a lot, so exiting out the stars is a lot more work than the satellites.

↳ reply 2 — happytoexplain:

Its parameters are very well described and the result is beautiful (visually), interesting, and provocative. Yes, people will misinterpret all sorts of things like this, but I don't know what else the author could have done besides not create it at all, for fear of... these accusations?

Top #3 — arjie:

This is awesome. How far we have come in the last century. How much farther we have to go. We will conquer the skies, and then the stars.

I remember thinking when I was a child how exciting the future was going to be. I had a bunch of these books talking about space and ships and stuff. Well, the future lived up to billing. We got there.

↳ reply — orangecat:

I hope to live long enough to see the part of The Expanse's title sequence where the moon lights up.

item.title: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
item.description: 555 points, 118 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (alpinelinux.org)

→ HN comments  ·  555 points  ·  118 comments

Top #1 — NewJazz:

musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.

Does anyone know why musl does this? Are they the only C library that behaves this way?

For a C library that famously tries to adhere to POSIX as much as possible, this seems like a crazy choice. From POSIX standard:

Upon successful completion, crypt() shall return a pointer to the encoded string. The first two bytes of the returned value shall be those of the salt argument. Otherwise, it shall return a null pointer and set errno to indicate the error.

https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/c...

↳ reply 1 — hnfong:

There's a very detailed trace of how the bug was developed over decades at sshhole.com and the relevant discussion in https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50378228

↳↳ reply — NewJazz:

Thanks yeah just woke up, finished making my way through the single-article website and still unclear if other libcs do the same thing (the article says libxcrypt picked it up, but only after musl did it).

↳↳↳ reply — NewJazz:

Some more clarity ... Multiple implementations have these sentinel values (not OpenBSD). But unfortunately only musl had a sentinel value that was also used in shadow files...

https://hachyderm.io/@ncopa@fosstodon.org/117564809789053485

↳ reply 2 — worksonmine:

Apparently because some devs didn't check for NULL which resulted in crashes. Weird choice to fix other peoples' bad programming by deviating from the spec.

↳ reply 3 — api:

TBH that sounds like a straight up bug in that it deviates dangerously from the spec.

Top #2 — 0127:

IMO this is where languages like Rust shine. The design patterns built into the language for handling errors (Result) - force you to handle errors / function results with sentinels, null pointers, or errnos are so much more error prone than handling a Result<T,E> using a match statement.

crypt() returning `*` is insane especially since these kinds of sentinels are all over /etc/passwd

↳ reply 1 — adrianN:

I guess this is where the culture around rust shines. You can write crypt that returns a string in rust just fine, just like you can write crypt that returns a tagged union in C. Cultural differences and syntactic sugar change which version is idiomatic.

I suppose if people started writing lots of code that crashed on error in Rust some enterprising developer might improve the function to always return a non-error value and set it to ‘*’ in error cases.

↳↳ reply — mort96:

The culture is downstream of the design IMO. In general, people write the API that is obvious. In C, returning a string is obvious, while defining a custom OptionalString type is high friction. In Rust, returning Option<String> is as easy and obvious as returning a String.

↳↳↳ reply — asveikau:

In a C function returning a string, two or three idioms are common for signalling an error.

One is to return NULL for errors.

Another is to make the string result a parameter and use a return code to signal error.

A third, less common but still out there, is an error parameter.

Failure to observe these is on the caller. Forcing the caller to consider the error is probably where rust shines.

But a good C programmer is thinking about these idioms when they encounter a function signature for the first time, or they write one.

↳ reply 2 — spullara:

always has amazed me that there was so much hate for java checked exceptions where handling errors ought to be the norm.

Top #3 — drob518:

Given Alpine’s broad use in the Docker ecosystem, this is going to hit a lot of folks, I think.

↳ reply 1 — apexalpha:

People generally don't expose SSH from within a Docker container I think.

↳↳ reply — eddyfromtheblok:

no, ssh INTO a running alpine container. who runs sshd in a container when you can just attach a terminal?

↳↳↳ reply — folmar:

you'll be surprised, ssh gives more ergonomic terminal, multiple connections, more convenient file sync and so on

↳ reply 2 — NewJazz:

Eh, most folks aren't hosting ssh servers with alpine containers and password auth enabled.

item.title: September in Servo: <progress>, rounded rectangles, and more
item.description: 175 points, 42 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (servo.org)

→ HN comments  ·  175 points  ·  42 comments

Top #1 — porphyra:

Servo is really great: Rust seems like a no brainer choice for a modern web engine, and its clean, performance-focused design from the ground up is wonderful.

But it seems really hard for it to get anywhere just based on occasional contributions from volunteers. I was actually quite surprised that basic functionality like <progress> and the :checked attribute were not even supported prior to this release.

Servo got 527 commits, while Chromium has over 20,000 commits.

↳ reply 1 — btown:

Part of this, as others have noted, is due to: https://book.servo.org/policy/ai-usage.html

> Can I submit a PR that includes code generated by AI tools?

> No. This includes (but is not limited to) all generative AI tools like Claude, Codex, ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, and Windsurf.

For something like a browser, this de facto limits the set of people who can contribute to something that touches the layout engine (e.g. the ineffable but brilliant https://github.com/servo/servo/blob/main/components/layout/f...) to just those already familiar with the code.

A much better middle ground IMO would be to quarantine first-time committers behind an AI-generated-PRs-will-not-be-reviewed policy, but to allow those who understand and respect the cycle enough to get PRs accepted, to begin using AI to give the team leverage. Without some kind of policy like that, Servo's sadly going to fall behind literally any other open-source project that people could dedicate their time towards.

↳↳ reply — fabrice_d:

Servo is already lacking reviewers. How would accepting AI contributions help?

↳ reply 2 — fabrice_d:

There are not just volunteer contributions, but also people working full time on Servo: some at Igalia, and some at Huawei at least.

Top #2 — robin_reala:

Remember that if you value Servo you can sponsor them, details at https://servo.org/sponsorship/

Top #3 — shakna:

Progress got my attention.

As an on-again off-again project, I've been building an incremental game that is pretty much just hundreds of progress bars - a little bit out of the norm for the browser.

Firefox everything renders smoothly and gently.

Chrome chugs, skips paints, delays animation frames, skips some events, and batches others.

Game uses a few features that aren't in Servo yet... But maybe I can tweak it...

item.title: MCP Explained
item.description: 225 points, 109 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (mcp-explained.com)

→ HN comments  ·  225 points  ·  109 comments

Top #1 — nater5000:

This is too dense. You might as well just post some Python code with sufficient comments to get the same point across. I think a nicely written article with a few diagrams would go a long way. Sometimes less is more.

MCPs don't really need this level of technical explanations (it's basically just a REST API with standardized endpoints for discovery aimed at agents), and AI agents really do lack in the taste dimension when it comes to these things.

↳ reply 1 — jrmg:

Yeah, this feels like one of those ‘explainers’ that feel like they are great to someone who already knows how the system works, but don’t actually work for newbies because they tacitly assume knowledge of the shape of the system that seems ‘obvious’ to someone steeped in it.

↳↳ reply — bityard:

This is a problem with most docs I encounter. _Good_ documentation should also teach the user how to use the thing, not simply end up as glorified out-of-band code comments.

↳↳↳ reply — Geezus_42:

I found that it's a mistake I would often make when writing documentation about something I deeply understand. I forget the questions that led me to that understanding. Now I make a conscious effort to think about the knowledge of the intended audience. I still miss things, but that's why it's good to have other people review.

↳ reply 2 — WhitneyLand:

To me the writing itself seems pretty economical.

From your comment, I expected to be annoyed by a bunch of slop or obscurities.

My guess is the writing did not come straight out of an LLM and was carefully curated.

If I’m wrong I’d love to have the style prompt.

↳ reply 3 — Aurornis:

> it's basically just a REST API

The opening has 1 paragraph and 5 table entries. One of them is “Not REST”

It’s a little scary that this was considered too dense or complex because the basics were explained in something that could be read in 1 minute. That still wasn’t enough to stop the top HN comment (as I write this) from calling it too dense and giving incorrect information that is immediately refuted by skimming the top part of the article.

Top #2 — Zaheer:

These vibe code explainers look nice on the surface but actually make things even more confusing. There's an element of curating which information to present and when that doesn't come across here.

↳ reply 1 — pllbnk:

Agree. These LLM-generated explainers tend to be useful only to the person who prompted for that explainer. That person knows what's unclear to them, they have their internal mind model that is known only to them and they can refine the explainer to their liking and keep prompting until it looks the way they want it to look and explains concepts how they want them explained. I use these all the time but see no reason for sharing something that is a couple prompts away for anyone else.

↳ reply 2 — truetraveller:

Hey Zaheer, am actually making something that is a "manual explainer maker". super simple but very nice. Will msg you later to solicit feedback. Anyone wants more info, DM me: http://x.com/realmustafamoon/

Top #3 — ndriscoll:

Are MCP calls composable in e.g. codex yet? e.g. can a model pipe a jira MCP call to grep or sed, or at least into a file? Last I looked at MCP it was just a vastly worse version of curl, .netrc, and some short text files describing calls (which are themselves greppable). Is there anything useful beyond that that I'm missing?

↳ reply 1 — zzbzq:

Last I checked it still doesn't. A skill that tells your client to call a CLI, and uses the help menus for progressive disclosure, benchmarks better. Developers noticed this immediately and there is sort of an anti-MCP sentiment. The protocol was probably largely conceived for non-coding agents run by non-coders.

In theory the agents could just natively know how to do this better, to get exactly the composability you want. In fact, you could probably just write a CLI mcp-caller and tell the agent to only call MCPs via that, and boom you're done.

Where MCP does come back into the picture even for coders is a more controlled way to break a sandbox.

What I will also say is it matters less and less. It's the usual bitter lesson. The models are just getting so much better all attempts to optimize everything are a drop in the bucket.

↳↳ reply — jameshart:

Too much exposure to local coding assistants seems to lead developers to assume that all agents typically operate in an environment where they have a full shell, with the ability to write arbitrary python scripts and curl commands and execute them.

Consider an agent which doesn’t have those tools though. MCPs are a great way to give them constrained access to remote resources.

↳↳↳ reply — ndriscoll:

It's more that I'd immediately ask why they don't. Obviously having some interpreter is going to make the model much more capable of context management and just analysis, so at the very least, it should be able to pipe MCP calls into e.g. a python interpreter with no IO other than stdin/stdout.

↳ reply 2 — nickstinemates:

What you want is Swamp - https://swamp-club.com. It was built for this.

item.title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
item.description: 277 points, 246 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:

→ HN comments  ·  277 points  ·  246 comments

Top #1 — ChrisMarshallNY:

> When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. None of these advanced algorithms have ever noticed this simple pattern.

Same here.

I think the songs get pushed by who pays to push, and most of those songs have vocals.

↳ reply 1 — _the_inflator:

Another one here. Vocal techno is a pain in my ears. There are few exceptions like in Bonzai Records classic tracks like “Let there be house.” or Emmanuel Top. These male voices are more aggressive and are helping to inject some additional energy into the songs, while female voices seem to drain it.

Goth industrial stuff from like the female singer from L’Âme Immortelle was a nice exception with “Bitterkeit”.

↳↳ reply — fierycatnet:
