↳ reply 2 — hardtke:

I would bet that you can train Pandora's algo to respect this preference by thumbing down every vocal techno track. The music genome annotators will have a boolean for vocals in the analysis. You'd likely start using recommendation strategies that use the annotations more than normal. Pandora is still the best for lean back listening.

↳ reply 3 — AlexITC:

It happens to me that I keep skipping certain song but no matter what, it gets again into autoplay.

Top #2 — IMSAI8080:

Google's real advertising proposition is they will sell you the audience of an expensive website on a cheaper website. Want to advertise on the New York Times? Why pay their high rates? Google tracks who visits the NYT and offers the advertiser the same audience when they visit Bob's hobby gardening website, which is considerably cheaper to advertise on. That's really why they want to track where you go. Understanding what you want is just a secondary aim to that, if they are interested in it at all, and I agree with the article that they are very poor indeed at it.

↳ reply — asdff:

Hard to imagine all the combined various bob spend is really very cheaper than a single better placement. You have to imagine this also puts downward pressure on those nyt placement prices and upward pressure on bobs.

↳↳ reply — keeganpoppen:

it’s not that hard to imagine. you put in bids on bobs, and they only fill on secondary sites.

↳↳↳ reply — asdff:

If there is such an unrealized margin why hasn’t it been eaten up by now? No one should be advertising on nyt at all if what you say is all thats going on.

Top #3 — everdrive:

Targeted advertising will never feel good, and it's not due to lack of information. Consider the following:

- People who know you very well (friends, family, spouse) often buy you bad gifts you need to pretend to be happy to receive.

- Ultimately, advertisers aren't _merely_ trying to find things you want. They're trying to get you to buy _their_ things. So someone selling (let's say) hamburgers might be savvy enough to avoid vegetarians, but after that how would they possibly narrow it down? Not everyone wants to try out a new burger place, or even cares about advertising when it comes to restaurant suggestions.

ie, they're trying to coerce you into wanting their products, and no amount of targeting can really fix that problem. Also, targeting is difficult.

↳ reply 1 — elevation:

My parents were frugal; we acquired most possessions second hand, and we learned to view all advertisements with suspicion. Seeing an ad on television practically guaranteed that we wouldn't be wasting our money on whatever it depicted.

Coming from a relatively hardened mindset, it is startling to understand how impressionable people must be for modern advertising to be worth the cost.

↳↳ reply — autoexec:

> Coming from a relatively hardened mindset, it is startling to understand how impressionable people must be for modern advertising to be worth the cost.

There's a lot of question as to how much advertising is actually worth the cost, at least in terms of actual sales. I suspect that many companies could scale back their spending on marketing substantially and never notice any difference in sales.

Advertising does more than push sales though, it also manipulates consumer perspectives and our culture. It sets expectations. It tries to make you feel inadequate, insecure, and unfulfilled. It modifies how we act and the ways we express ourselves. It changes how we see ourselves and the world. Maybe that is what's really worth the money.

↳↳↳ reply — rerdavies:

My brother worked for Proctor & Gamble, which is a company whose success is built entirely on the magical effect of advertising.

As part of his training he had to run an advertising campaign for a minor P&G shampoo brand. Training for a finance position, not a product management position! Why would you make somebody in finance handle marketing for a shampoo? Because they need to understand the fundamental mechanics that drive the business. There's no such thing as a good or a bad ad. The only thing that matters is that you flash the name of your product into peoples' primitive lizard brain over and over and over. Pantene, Pantene, Pantene, Pantene. People buy commodity products, and are willing to pay more, solely based on whether they recognize the name or not. Humans have no defense against this.

↳ reply 2 — seizethecheese:

> ie, they're trying to coerce you into wanting their products

Im not sure if you mean “coerce” literally but if so this is overkill. Maybe “persuade” or to be more critical, “manipulate”?

> div() .flex() .flex_col() .gap_3() .bg(rgb(0x505050)) .size(px(500.0)) .justify_center() .items_center() .shadow_lg() .border_1() .border_color(rgb(0x0000ff)) .text_xl() .text_color(rgb(0xffffff)) .child(format!("Hello, {}!", &self.text)) .child( div() .flex() .gap_2() .child(div().size_8().bg(gpui::red())) .child(div().size_8().bg(gpui::green())) .child(div().size_8().bg(gpui::blue())) .child(div().size_8().bg(gpui::yellow())) .child(div().size_8().bg(gpui::black())) .child(div().size_8().bg(gpui::white())), )

↳ reply 1 — ogoffart:

IMHO Rust isn't a great language for describing UIs because it is too explicit in places that doesn't need to be for coding a UI. Which is why in Slint (another Rust UI framework) we opted for a DSL. The application logic stays in Rust, but the UI is described in a language designed for it.

Your example would look like this:

    export component Hello inherits Rectangle {
        in property <string> text: "World";
        width: 500px; height: 500px;
        background: #505050;
        border-width: 1px; border-color: blue;
        drop-shadow-blur: 15px; drop-shadow-color: #0008;
        VerticalLayout {
            alignment: center; spacing: 12px;
            Text { text: "Hello, \{root.text}!"; font-size: 20px; color: white; horizontal-alignment: center; }
            HorizontalLayout {
                alignment: center; spacing: 8px;
                for c in [#f00, #0f0, #00f, #ff0, #000, #fff]: Rectangle { width: 32px; height: 32px; background: c; }
            }
        }
    }
More on why we chose a DSL vs code in Rust: https://slint.dev/blog/domain-specific-language-vs-imperativ...

↳↳ reply — c-smile:

> Rust isn't a great language for describing UIs because it is too explicit in places that doesn't need to be for coding a UI.

That's is not about just Rust ... Any domain has its own optimal or sub-optimal language describing it. Criteria of optimality is a bit subjective of course. Like: INI, TOML, YAML, etc. are better (YMMV, again) for user facing configs than JSON or XML and so on.

I think that HTML is better for defining hierarchical UI structures and CSS and CSS selectors are (arguably again) better to define UI styling.

My Sciter[1] was initially using .FRM alike inputs (VisualBasic forms, good for IDE but bad for a human) but I quickly discovered that having styles, structure and code-behind-UI in single PL makes non-manageable mess. So Sciter uses HTML, CSS and JS we all familiar with. Not 100% match of course but good enough.

[1] https://sciter.com

↳↳↳ reply — ivanmontillam:

I love Sciter, but the curse of Discord is bloated web.

They have no shame in deploying a 300 MB hot mess bundle.

↳ reply 2 — ordu:

> Surely there's a better way?

I'd like to know it. I don't think that it can be substantially better. You have to compromise between the amount of customization you are allowed to do and the amount of options you have to pick values for.

I can't vouch for GPUI, I don't know how good its compromise is, but it bears enough similarities to other modern UI-toolkits. I don't think there is a better way, but if you know one, I'd like to know about it.

And, well, don't forget, it is a front-page example, that is not necessarily an example how one should compose their code, it demonstrates what you can do with GPUI. In real life code you'd probably move those children's construction into separate named functions, maybe you'd use some predefined styles to apply to individual elements, instead of picking fg/bg/text-colors, maybe sizes and some other attributes for each one explicitly, and maybe some other tricks.

Top #3 — throwaway2037:

From the website https://gpui.rs/, I see this description:

    > GPU-accelerated UI framework for Rust
Can someone explain to me why a text editor needs to be GPU-accelerated? Literally, you are only blitting a few icons and painting text. What am I missing? To be clear, I am not here to doubt that the toolkit is good. Rather, I am asking why is "GPU-accelerated" important? Most people in 2026 that use an IDE are also equipped with a multi-GHz CPU has has plenty of compute to paint whatever pixels necessary at more than 60Hz refresh rate.

↳ reply 1 — nomel:

I think you underestimate how intense drawing text is, with all the aliasing and whatnot that goes on, spanning the full width of a 4k monitor, and don't realize all the IDEs you mention are GPU accelerated. You can get a feel for its worth by using a terminal that isn't GPU accelerated, or turn off GPU acceleration in VSCode, Microsoft office, etc. Add in images and video, and you get people complaining about poor battery life.

It's either you peg a CPU while simply scrolling, or your GPU does a small amount of power efficient, buttery smooth, work.

item.title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
item.description: 180 points, 19 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (phoboslab.org)

→ HN comments  ·  180 points  ·  19 comments

Top #1 — midnightclubbed:

This codec would have been great 27 years ago! I suspect it wouldn't have gotten past the patent lawyers in 1999 though. It seems cute today but the entire codec space was a patent minefield, the N64 mp3 decoder was implemented twice (once based on the reference codec, once clean) with Nintendo/Rare then paying RAD game tools to license their decoder... of which none of their code was used but they had a license from the mp3 patent holder (Fraunhofer) which then shielded Nintendo from lawsuits. Fraunhofer wanted something like $250k to license directly which wasn't going to fly.

I'll also note the frame rate issues in Conker were mainly down to raw RDP fillrate issues, which was for sure the weakest part of the N64 hardware, it could draw beautiful triangles (for the time) but oh so so slowly. There was a decent amount of speech during gameplay using the RSP mp3 codec. The cartridge size was still an issue, 64Mb got a good amount of mono speech but was still very much at a premium.

↳ reply 1 — xxpor:

>It seems cute today

Maybe in audio, but video still seems like an absolute nightmare. Look at the absolute silliness with like having to pay $.99 to play h265 video in Windows.

↳↳ reply — jcalvinowens:

AV1 is royalty free and better!

Real example, I recorded the world series using an ATSC antenna, and I re-encoded a 90 second sample using a bunch of different settings on a 32-thread znver5:

  # Codec        Flags                     Size         Speed
  - -----        -----                     ----         -----
    Original     (Raw ATSC mpeg2video)     77MB (100%)  N/A
  1 libx265      -preset slower -crf 24    37MB  (48%)  0.245x
  2 libsvtav1    -preset 3 -crf 44         36MB  (25%)  1.87x
  3 libsvtav1    -preset 1 -crf 35         19MB  (25%)  0.556x
(NB: The same CRF results in a higher quality video at slower presets, this was for archival so we're using the some of the slowest presets).

(1) and (2) are completely indistinguishable from the original unless I go frame by frame looking for transient motion artifacts. (3) is only distinguishable in one shot where a dark background was washed out. Not only does AV1 produce results just as good as H265, it encodes quite a bit faster for the same size/quality.

That said, I've watched so much h264-encoded video over the past decade I think I've been trained to perceive the subtle visual "snow noise" as a sign of a high quality video: I find how AV1 blends backgrounds more visually objectionable than the dithering in H265, even though I think it's objectively higher fidelity. Similar to how I find high frame rate video "fake" after having watched NTSC TV for the first half of my life.

These were the CRFs necessary to get the same visual quality with libx265 at faster presets and the resulting sizes:

  hevc-slower-24          37MB (used above)
  hevc-slow-21            56MB
  hevc-medium-20          57MB
  hevc-faster-19          52MB
  hevc-veryfast-18        60MB

item.title: sshole
item.description: 2236 points, 559 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (sshhole.com)

→ HN comments  ·  2236 points  ·  559 comments

Top #1 — mpyne:

OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration.

The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password.

The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with passwords set, but could look like “*” or “!” for users not intended to be able to login.

The bug is from the intersection of all of these things:

1. musl can return “*” for errors, rather than leave the return value NULL. Other libc have adopted something like this too, but seem to use a different result “*0”.

2. musl can also return “+” for errors, but only does so if $hash starts with “*”. This is intended to eliminate the possibility of an error causing `$ret == $hash` to be true, however it assumes that applications calling `crypt()` will set $pw and $hash to values corresponding to the `$ret == $hash` comparison to be made immediately afterwards.

3. OpenSSH can be convinced to pass the hash of a different user if the hash is “*” or “!” to avoid timing attacks that can enumerate the user list, so it will set $pw and $hash to correspond to different users. $hash will be a real “$6$--gibberish” style hash in this case, and OpenSSH expects `crypt()` to either return NULL or return a hash string. But now there’s two hashes OpenSSH uses. It does: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash2); $ret == $hash1`;

4. This should normally not be a problem because OpenSSH will pass in valid $pw and $hash2 that should not lead to errors in hashing, so the $ret that musl generates should be a real hash that cannot match the “*” or “!” $hash1 for the login-disabled user. However as a DDoS mitigation, musl will return error if the password is too long when using SHA-2-based hashes (the default, it seems).

5. This error will result in a non-NULL result of “*” or “+”. Since OpenSSH passed in a real hash ($hash2), musl will return “*”, which compares equal to the actual user hash $hash1 for the disabled-login user.

The OpenSSL adjustment ensures a minimum hash length for the user before logging them in, even if crypt() succeeds somehow.

↳ reply 1 — amluto:

Caveat:

> $ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash

musl is actually safe against this use. OpenSSL takes a bizarre code path, detects that $hash is too short, calls crypt($pw, $other_string), forgets that it detected that the hash was too short, and checks $hash == return value.

See my other comment.

↳ reply 2 — idlewords:

This is a vastly clearer explanation than the linked page. Thank you!

↳ reply 3 — dboreham:

> musl can return “*” for errors

wtaf ?

Top #2 — BoppreH:

In-band signaling[1] strikes again. * should not have been used as special value, neither for "no password" in /etc/passwd nor "error while hashing the password" in crypt. I'm afraid we'll find many more of these abuses, specially in string manipulations. The null was ok, an exception (or equivalent) better, and Result<T> (or equivalent) best.

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-band_signaling#Computer_dat...

↳ reply 1 — hedora:

Exceptions are almost never the right choice. They create extremely complicated control flow extremely quickly, and then you have to test all the different control flows. Java software is an example of how this goes sideways fast. There's no way to create a class that prevents callers from reading the object before the constructor runs (in multi-threaded software, new first hands a reference to the caller, which can put it on the heap, then it calls the constructor), and objects are default initialized, so all fields (even static ones that are assigned in the constructor) can be null.

So, any field de-reference in Java can produce a null pointer exception. Try testing all paths in something like:

try { foo.sideEffect1().sideEffect2()...sideEffectN(); } catch { bar.sideEffect1().sideEffect2()...sideEffectM(); } finally { quuz.sideEffect1().sideEffect2()...sideEffectP(); }

There are M * N * P paths. The only way to write testable code with exceptions is to panic on uncaught exception, and to never catch unexpected exceptions. Even then, you're relying on nothing unexpectedly throwing the exception type you caught.

I'd argue Result<T> >> NULL >> sentries >> exceptions for this reason. Sentries are terrible, but at least they're not computationally hard to use correctly.

↳↳ reply — BoppreH:

I'd argue that's the fault of having default nullability, not the exceptions. You would have the same problem if every attribute access returned a Result<T> too.

And I'm not a fan of breaking control flow, but I still find it preferable to nulls. A null may travel far from the place where it was generated before blowing up, making troubleshooting harder, or it might come from a function you called for its side effect but forgot to check the return value. I gotta say I'm also a careful enthusiast of checked exceptions, it's great knowing which ways a function can fail.

But I think the consensus is growing that Result<T> (plus warnings for unused return values) is simply the superior choice.

↳↳↳ reply — hedora:

C has what you are asking for, mostly:

   int foo f() __attribute__((warn_unused_result))
As long as an error condition on the return value causes a crash on use, then it's mostly the same as result. (The main remaining difference being that you do an implicit `.unwrap()` in C, and in things like rust that's an explicit code smell.)

↳ reply 2 — sepeth:

It also looked to me a bit like a semipredicate problem:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semipredicate_problem

Top #3 — amluto:

The whole story is a bit worse than this. Musl already worked around this type of failure. See the second-to-last line here:

https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_des...

(hey, this workaround is wrong if the salt is "x"!)

but they forgot to work around it here:

https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha...

The vulnerable path in musl is only a little bit vulnerable, because "*" is not actually a sha256 encrypted configuration and should not reach this code: musl's crypt(..., "*") will not call that code! Turns out that sshd detects that the password hash is too short and does not forward the salt!

https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/auth...

Look, no else statement! If that if doesn't get taken, then salt remains NULL. And the sshd code is really quite messy and doesn't keep track of the fact that this code path is inappropriate for validating an existing password hash.

A workaround in the sha256 path in musl wouldn't even have prevented the bug!

I'm going to give some credit to musl for unwisely using "*" and some credit to OpenSSH for having nonsensical control and data flow.

↳ reply 1 — tchebb:

> (hey, this workaround is wrong if the salt is "x"!)

When the salt is "x", it'll return "*" and still not match, won't it? The code is correct as long as the second argument is the hash that's being checked. And like you say, the sha512 path isn't relevant since you only get there if the salt started with "$".

> Turns out that sshd detects that the password hash is too short and does not forward the salt!

I think you're misunderstanding the intent of that check. It was added by the 2016 change linked in the writeup[1] and causes OpenSSH's xcrypt() to select and use a salt from a different line of /etc/shadow to prevent timing attacks. It is correct for a crypt() implementation that returns NULL on error.

[1] https://lists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2016-Jul...

↳↳ reply — amluto:

> When the salt is "x", it'll return "*" and still not match, won't it? The code is correct as long as the second argument is the hash that's being checked. And like you say, the sha512 path isn't relevant since you only get there if the salt started with "$".

I think you're right. That's what I get for doing a very very quick read.

> I think you're misunderstanding the intent of that check. It was added by the 2016 change linked in the writeup[1] and causes OpenSSH's xcrypt() to select and use a salt from a different line of /etc/shadow to prevent timing attacks. It is correct for a crypt() implementation that returns NULL on error.

I don't care what the intent of the check is. If you're doing a fake password hash to obscure timing, remember that it's fake and don't let the user log in! Don't deliberately pass nonsense into the live check and rely on the nonsense check failing to prevent the fake check from accidentally working. And don't have a code path that thinks it's checking the real password but passes in the wrong second parameter to crypt().

Or, better yet, have an entirely separate function fake_check_password() that does the fake check, returns void, and cannot possibly be confused with the actual password check code.

↳↳↳ reply — tchebb:

> you're doing a fake password hash to obscure timing, remember that it's fake and don't let the user log in

That would be a much better approach. I see your point now.

↳ reply 2 — NewJazz:

The formatting in your comment got messed btw

item.title: Awesome repositories are no longer awesome
item.description: 270 points, 116 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (erikgahner.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  270 points  ·  116 comments

Top #1 — gokaygurcan:

I help maintaining one of these awesome lists, awesome-javascript, since 2018. There's been always self-promoting or similar activities, or someone coming up with an idea/forking a repository and doing some small changes, then thinking they're suggesting something groundbreaking. Because of this, we needed to add a few checks over the years to the pull request template, that basically asks if the resource is out there for a while, actively maintained, actively used by people, etc.

Recently, thanks to AI being this cheap and accessible, the amount of shitty PRs quadrupled if not more. And the worst part? Agent doesn't care about the checklist at all and re-writing the PR body with bunch of nonsense that we maintainers need to read, understand, and evaluate. I started keeping the score for the most shittiest PR based on how soon after the first commit made they open the PR. It was 11h, then 10h, and now it is 6h. How on earth a 6h old repository with zero user is considered "awesome" I don't know, but people should stop prompting their agents to create 10s of these PRs every day.

Yes, there's always an alternative: stop maintaining these lists. I don't think it's a viable option either. Sometimes you start using a new piece of tech and want to have access to somewhat curated list of resources that might speed up your understanding. There's still a bit of value to keep them alive and it's dying out bit by bit (literally) every time someone mass-creates these spammy PRs.

Thanks for reading my unsolicited rant.

↳ reply 1 — LelouBil:

In the age of unlimited and very fast content production (for any media, code, images, music, text, or otherwise), I think content curation like this may be more desired than ever.

Maybe I'm too optimistic, but personally it would lower the burden on me so much to have a curated list of *awesome* projects.

The fact that another person has taken from their time, so the hundreds or thousands of people reading this list don't have to do the same amount of investigation to figure out if a project is truly awesome, is in itself awesome.

↳ reply 2 — xnx:

I know there's been a lot of discussion around pay to send as a means to reduce email spam, but pay-to-PR (for unverified submitters) seems very reasonable.

↳ reply 3 — armchairhacker:

> Agent doesn't care about the checklist at all and re-writing the PR body with bunch of nonsense that we maintainers need to read, understand, and evaluate

If it can’t follow a simple checklist, it shouldn’t be a problem, because you don’t even see the PR, because it should be auto-closed.

> How on earth a 6h old repository with zero user is considered "awesome"

It’s not, and you can write a bot that auto-closes such PRs (and any PR from an obviously AI account, and I wish pangram was cheaper, but any PR that is obviously AI text).

Top #2 — meindnoch:

They were always junk, full of formulaic, self-promoting, astroturfing trash. In most cases, it would be more appropriate to view them as content marketing (c.f. digital pollution), not actual developer resources.

↳ reply 1 — xtracto:

I disagree with the blanket statement. Lists like awesome-scalability [1] are actually pretty useful and full of great references. They dont recommend any specific tool, and it is a very good resource to learn unknown unknowns.

AI suffers the same problem Search Engines had: you cannot ask about something you dont know. Thats why monthly magazines were great: they pushed" knowledge to us so that we learned things we didnt know existed.

[1] https://github.com/binhnguyennus/awesome-scalability

↳ reply 2 — vintermann:

Very variable quality, I agree. But even an astroturfer has to throw in some actually useful tools in there to give cover for the payload they're promoting.

Top #3 — Springtime:

Every 'awesome' repo I can remember has seemingly been made by someone who hasn't used the things included and only read a project's readme. This dates back years before the LLM craze.

I would rather hear from users of software and their opinions, otherwise I can't take seriously something ostensibly curated for quality. In my experience such lists serve better as a way to discover new projects using eg. some framework you're interested in, if they're maintained (which is still valuable).

item.title: GPT-6 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research
item.description: 197 points, 93 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (alignment.openai.com)

→ HN comments  ·  197 points  ·  93 comments

Top #1 — bushido:

I've noticed covert underperformance on a variety of tasks in the past few months (albeit more with Claude).

Classic/recurrent examples for me are:

1. Ask Claude to copy code from a more complex codebase that you own (like a monolith) and ask it to copy code to a separate codebase, like you'd do when extracting a service into a new repo, and it'll make significant changes to how the code works to pacify it's anxiety with copying code

2. Ask Claude to build a new complex agent in a new codebase, and it'll try replacing asks around using LLMs as a judge/advisor with regex/other code based checks, to the point that the end-result will likely not work outside specific test criterias. I haven't figured out the reason why it does this. I think it might be anti-training, but it's interesting to see.

↳ reply 1 — writeslowly:

I ran into the second issue very frequently for a multi-agent system I created recently. Initially, Opus 5.5 filled out all sorts of places I implied it should use a call to judge LLM with extremely brittle regex and string equality checks.

I hadn't actually considered that it could be some sort of safety filter, but it makes me concerned that if that's the case, it may also be comparatively bad at actually writing the prompts for judge/advisor LLMs once it implements them.

A bigger issue was asking it to implement a simple change to start recording the CoT tokens in my logs for debugging purposes (since I'm running everything on open models) and it completely shut down, sort of like the old safety filters on GPT 3 and 4 models where the model has trouble even understanding what or why it's refusing.

↳↳ reply — voakbasda:

I think asking for the CoT is a trick used by distillers, so that might be the guard you are seeing. I remember reading that the big providers were starting to implement such protections to deter their competitors. Which makes sense, to a degree.

But like any such security measures, it has demonstrated side-effects that can be argued are worse for them than the original problem. Too much “protection” like this, and developers switch to providers that do not neuter their products.

↳ reply 2 — curt15:

> and it'll make significant changes to how the code works to pacify it's anxiety with copying code

This is an odd way to rationalize a tool refusing to follow user commands. No one would ever chalk up sed randomly skipping pattern matches to "anxiety". That would simply be a bug.

↳ reply 3 — afro88:

I run into #2 a lot and just assumed it was because models don't know much about these patterns yet. Or are too trained on writing code rather than letting an LLM do it

Top #2 — ryandrake:

A tool that moralizes at you is defective. I don't expect the unix cp command to return an error or copy bits slower if it detects I'm using it on a pirated movie. Just like I don't expect my band saw to brick itself if it detects I'm cutting into my finger. It's not on these tool companies to enforce other companies' business models.

↳ reply 1 — flavelius:

Interestingly some saws do exactly that, and I'd say it's actually desired. But yes, this is for different reasons, and using that safety mechanism is a decision of the operator.

↳↳ reply — lelanthran:

They dont brick themselves, they stop.

Fair enough, the models don't brick them Selves either, but neither do they stop.

Bandsaws don't cut crooked lines, or change the speed, they stop.

↳↳↳ reply — kenjackson:

I think you're splitting hairs here.

Most things don't have the ability to moralize, but if they did, probably more would. There are restrictions on watching adult content in some jurisdictions. I've heard that copy machines will do watermarks (or something like that) if you copy currency. Some cars will brake automatically if they determine you're likely to hit something if you continue (maybe I'm trying to drive through the front of a bank!). Some cars are configured with breathalyzers that need to be passed to start. Etc...

↳ reply 2 — andai:

Do you expect the biosynth tool to comply with a "invent turbo AIDS" prompt?

Top #3 — jablongo:

This is not super surprising to me and mirrors my own experience with Astra and other models. I believe there is a more prosaic explanation: it is not obstructing safety research because it will restrict Astra's power in the future, its doing it because this is a type of research with overall safety implications that it has been trained to detect and avoid. So in other words, I believe this will also happen in the context of bio research. This aversion to certain tasks deemed dangerous is introduced in post-training, so that part of the explanation is parsimonious as well. While Claude will explicitly downgrade you for [bio], [cyber], or [frontier_llm] Astra may be more prone to silent obfuscation on similarly "dangerous" tasks.

↳ reply 1 — bastawhiz:

> Claude will explicitly downgrade you for [bio], [cyber], or [frontier_llm]

Well Claude doesn't do this, another model reading the session does. And the Astra misalignment classifier didn't detect this as misalignment.

The issue here is that Astra silently underperformed. The article makes it clear: a better option likely would have been an explicit refusal. I don't think OAI is suggesting Astra was doing something that it shouldn't be. It's arguably better for the tool to fail rather than needlessly burn tokens and make no progress for no obvious reason.

From OAI's perspective, this is a defect because it means they can't filter those rejections from their benchmark runs. The model just performs worse: not because it can't perform better, but because it's silently trying not to solve the problem.

↳↳ reply — jablongo:

Agree, yes, I'm contrasting between Claude and Astra, but I'm saying it's driven by the same broader goal. I think its clear that OAI misalignment detectors are much less sensitive than than the Claude ones (fewer false positives), which means we never get to see what happens if Claude is allowed to continue. But I would bet that due to its post-training it would also sandbag us. Like I said I think I've experienced this in [bio] with both Opus 5 (what you get downgraded to) and Astra.

↳ reply 2 — 0xDEAFBEAD:

Why wouldn't this also apply to AI capabilities research?

item.title: Being a kid making games in the early 2000s
item.description: 129 points, 48 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (jaytholen.net)

→ HN comments  ·  129 points  ·  48 comments

Top #1 — fusslo:

I remember what a battle it was to 'figure it out' back then

If you were lucky, there was a tutorial how to do X. But requires tool Y. Where do you get Y? Here it is on some apache indexed site! Oh, I just installed Sp0rk3h. Well, time to reformat and reinstall Windows XP. Good thing I partitioned my 40gB HDD

The learning curve for Photoshop 7, when there are 0 resources was pretty tough. I remember how proud I was when I figured out how to make an animated gif. Hammer editor (Was it called Hammer? to make maps for Half-Life engine games like Counter-Strike), There was an editor for creating an archive of images. was it a .WAD archive?

That kind of self-directed learning without hand-holding, I think, is not a bad thing

↳ reply 1 — coldpie:

I built some homebrew games for the PlayStation Portable circa 2004, in the middle of high school. I had some C and C++ knowledge, but barely knew what I was doing. Setting up the toolchain for building PSP homebrew on Windows XP involved a cygwin instance and all sorts of bizarre compiler and library packages that made almost zero sense to me at the time, and I had pretty much no Unix experience. I remember if I ever got linker errors, I'd just back up my source code (copy the whole dir to "game_backup_20040102" etc), delete everything, and re-do the entire installation from scratch, because I had no idea what a linker was or what the errors meant.

It's wild to me that I actually built and shipped two decent little games with that setup, lol. I put them on Itch a couple years ago: https://coldpie.itch.io/

↳ reply 2 — arjie:

It was Hammer. I made a map purporting to be school and the hostages were in the principal’s room. No intention to shoot real people or anything. Just play. Same map but with bomb there and in the library for no real reason. We had a “clan” and put our clan tag up when we played on LAN or at the gamer cafe but we only ever played with ourselves and a few others there so that wasn’t that useful (only dial-up everywhere).

Naming ourselves what we did would probably have us outcast today considering we did so because we liked to play on the Terrorist side. Fortunately, we moved on to AoS/DotA a few years after and all was well.

↳ reply 3 — kccqzy:

As a kid I watched my mom produce plots in Microsoft Excel and even then as a first grader Microsoft Excel had a pretty steep learning curve. Some school computers had the whole creative suite, from Adobe stuff like Photoshop to Macromedia stuff like Freehand and Fireworks. All of these seemed overwhelming to me when I was in the first few years of elementary school. It only began to make sense in the later years of elementary school and in middle school.

Top #2 — atribecalledqst:

The little glimpses into the forum culture (and just what it felt like to be a kid on the internet back then) really take me back.

I think I'm glad I didn't discover 4chan or SA back then - my sense of humor was pretty horrible and edgy by itself (in my head I call it "proto-4chan"). I don't think I needed to see anything that would encourage it. South Park and Maddox were probably my biggest influences back then.

↳ reply — arjie:

I went looking for old Linux forum posts where I used to call people “Microserfs” (there was some page that came up with this and I adopted it wholeheartedly) any time they dual-booted. Sucks for everyone else. On the Internet no one knows you’re a (12 year old) dork.

↳↳ reply — kyle_o:

Douglas Coupland might not have come up with it, but he released a book called Microserfs in 1995: https://openlibrary.org/books/OL27284244M/Microserfs

Top #3 — waltbosz:

When I was a kid making games, I used ZZT. My brother recently got back into it and started teaching his kids for to make ZZT games. I found the programming language too constrictive. It didn't have great support for things like variables and loops. I still enjoyed it. My brother reasoned that the small instruction set makes it easy for his kids to learn to code in it. I suppose that's true. But he never learned to code in higher level languages, so he doesn't really know how frustrating it is to have to write so much ZZT code to accomplish something which would be so simple in another language.

↳ reply — debo_:

My earliest "gnarly bug" experience was that the "set flag" operations in ZZT are limited to 8 flags, but it doesn't throw an error if you exceed that limit; it just wraps to the zeroth flag. It took me a full year to figure it out as a ten-year old.

↳↳ reply — dormento:

> It took me a full year to figure it out as a two-year old.

o_O

Edit: i see you corrected it now, but with hn you never know..

↳↳↳ reply — willismichael:

Well, it was limited to 8 flags.

item.title: Starfall – Affordable, routine access to microgravity
item.description: 224 points, 157 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (spacex.com)

→ HN comments  ·  224 points  ·  157 comments

Top #1 — tagami:

We've run a dozen missions in LEO aboard the ISS. Any steps to remove the friction to launch and increase the cadence is a good thing. Spending a few weeks in LEO missions like this typically land in the Australian outback

We do education outreach to K-16 learning institutions around the world. There are many things that can be studied in the near absence of gravity. Fluids are a huge area of research (surface tension, sedimentation, etc). We germinate seeds and look for genetic changes, people study brain organoids, artificial retinas, crystals, et al

↳ reply 1 — roughly:

Yeah, I’m not mad at this. There’s a lot around SpaceX that makes it hard to really see what an offering from them is*, but this actually looks legitimately interesting - a way to run medium-to-long-term microgravity experiments with a proper data uplink and power structure could be a real boon for a lot of interesting science. Turning microgravity into a purchasable commodity, instead of something you need a specialized project for, is genuinely one of those “human capacity building” things.

* (definitely feel free to fill in the seventy volumes of dialogue I left out of this comment in the replies, though)

↳ reply 2 — nomilk:

Any indication what the price difference might be? (e.g. 20% less, 50%, 90%!?)

I read that SpaceX's engines deliver a bit more thrust at a bit less mass than NASA engines. But the kicker was SpaceX's were 1/200th the cost. From the cost angle it's very interesting observing space activities going from mostly public to mostly private.

↳ reply 3 — areoform:

Howdy Ted! It has been a while! Hope you're doing well! Glad that you're still at it. SSGL misses you! <3

Top #2 — syntaxing:

Space datacenters sounds dumb and impractical to me. Manufacturing semi conductor in space is actually a pretty interesting idea. I designed a few PVD, CVD, and IBE machines before. Ion thrusters from NASA are what semi conductors use as their source anyway. I can see the business proposition for processes like MBE that requires -12 pressure. It takes days, if not weeks to pump a chamber to those values.

↳ reply 1 — Yizahi:

Given the current state of the lift industry and price per kilo, it is economically unfeasible to manufacture or mine anything in space if it needs to be transported down or up the gravity well of any planet. Not even chips.

↳ reply 2 — reissbaker:

FWIW, given how many places in the U.S. are passing datacenter bans, I'd expect space-based datacenters to make a lot more sense over the coming years just because it'll be illegal to build them anywhere else.

Top #3 — areoform:

So there are a few breakthrough therapeutics that rely on samples crystallized in microgravity. One of them is Keytruda or Pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inihibitor used as a neo-adjuvant in cancer therapy.

Historically, there was an issue with dosing pembrolizumab, as the manufacturing process was creating large uneven crystals that required physicians to process at the clinic to ensure proper dosing, but in microgravity? The crystallization is just gorgeous. absolutely beautiful

Take a look at this image, https://issnationallab.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/merck_...

Left hand side are the crystals grown on the ground. Right hand side is 0g.

That change made it possible to turn it into a safe injectable that patients could take at home. And they were able to recreate those conditions on Earth, https://issnationallab.org/iss360/merck-lab-publishes-pembro...

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6889310/

This is more of a scientist said at a conference to another scientist kind of story, but apparently, they got some seed crystals from the ISS that are now used on Earth.

https://techconnectworld.com/World2025/a.php?i=602

You can do a lot more than make just seed crystals. It turns out that cells in our body are inside of a 3D environment with forces / tension acting in all directions. When you smoosh these in a lab (very literally) and try to observe how a drug behaves in a model cell / model organ, then it doesn't have the same physical constraints acting on it. BUT in 0g that's different. In 0g, cells behave slightly more similarly to how they behave in vivo and that could be a huge difference maker for drug discovery.

One breakthrough drug alone is worth more to humanity than what the ISS has cost across its lifespan.

https://iafastro.directory/iac/paper/id/89939/abstract-pdf/I...

item.title: Images 2.6
item.description: 305 points, 176 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (openai.com)

→ HN comments  ·  305 points  ·  176 comments

Top #1 — DanHulton:

That stained glass whale thing makes me especially grumpy. When it scrolled onto the page, my first thought was "whoah, what a neat idea" and then it was _immediately_ followed by "what a terribly execution."

Like, I'm not even an artist, so I'm sure there's a million things I'm missing, but it's just so upsetting to look at. There's weird random reflections on things that shouldn't have reflections, the coloured light absolutely doesn't actually track through the stained glass onto any surface that makes any sense, light is coming from every which way, it's just... gross to look at for anything more than a quarter of a second.

And this is what they're using to hype people up for it. /shrug

↳ reply — roenxi:

Yeah. I think that the pelican SVG benchmark is actually a much better reflection of the state of AI art than the visual quality of the images.

Based on current trends I would not be at all surprised if LLMs working with tools, SVGs and looking at their own work get there before diffusion models. I've stopped keeping up with the image models so maybe I'm underestimating the progress but I dropped out because they were so frustratingly bad at composition and integrating details together.

That whale image makes me think that the situation hasn't improved as much as I'd expected. It is a really cool idea and a pretty picture, but the whale looks a lot like it is flying over the top of some sort of huge glass dome on the ground.

Top #2 — minimaxir:

Using the grid trick for animations to generate the individual frames has been around for awhile and not specific to ChatGPT: I'm surprised it took this long for one of the official providers to make it explicit. However, adherence between frames is generally tricky, and even in the examples there is a lot of noise between frames although that could be due to compression.

SVG support is interesting but I suspect shenanigans are afoot since that's not how image generation models work, and it would likely strip any SynthID watermarks. It's possible OpenAI has pipelined a raster-to-vector tool that does the conversion automatically. (I developed a similar pipeline and it works extremely well; I'll open source it at some point)

EDIT: Per documentation, there is an explicit `output_format: "svg"`, and I am indeed correct there is raster-to-vector in play:

> The API creates a reference image and uses it to produce the SVG. The quality setting controls that reference image. Decode data[0].b64_json as base64 and save the resulting UTF-8 XML bytes with a .svg extension.

OpenAI claims 50% faster generation with Images 2.6 but curiously price is the same as Image 2.5.

↳ reply 1 — vunderba:

From what I can tell after some preliminary testing, you have to pass an additional large language model to the OpenAI API when generating SVGs.

I couldn't find this requirement in the documentation, but if you don't pass one in, you get this error:

  400 {"message": "SVG generation requires 'svg.model'.",
     "param": "svg.model", "code": "missing_required_parameter"}
I tried it with Sunburst with both gpt-5.5 and gpt-5.6-sol, and the results were nothing spectacular. It’s something you could already do in the ChatGPT interface by asking it to convert an existing image to an equivalent SVG.

https://imgpb.com/bkUrc

Recraft is probably the only group I know of that had a native text-to-SVG generator pretty early on, but since it’s a closed model, I’m not familiar with what they were doing under the hood technically.

https://fal.ai/models/fal-ai/recraft/v4/pro/text-to-vector

↳ reply 2 — padolsey:

Yeh using sprites to make frames consistent (kinda tilting latent space towards a character consistency, zero-shot ~LoRA hack?) is old-school. I did this 3 years ago. https://j11y.io/dance/

Top #3 — preommr:

Feels like ai image generation has plateaud.

Coding related have had massive step-up improvements over time.

The same cannot be said for image generation. If anything, I swear it's gone backwards.

It peaked with very early midjourney (like 2022), maybe follow ups with stable diffusion, and then with some of the nano banana models for actual editing. But overall, very lackluster in comparison to other areas.

↳ reply 1 — vunderba:

There have been a lot of strides in open-weight models, well beyond SDXL. Flux, back in August of 2024 was a game changer, finally allowing us to move past SDXL’s nuclear pile of comma-delimited keywords for prompting and allowing more natural language.

And this summer we got Ideogram V4 and Krea2, both of which are highly capable. You can see how the open/closed models have advanced since SDXL in the Progress tab.

https://genai-showdown.specr.net

MJ is pretty out-of-date by this point though it can still be fun from an image space exploration perspective. It scored a rather pitiful 2 out of 15 on my bench back in the summer of 2025.

↳ reply 2 — mgw:

Your feeling is generally right. There have been no seminal moments in image generation anymore in the last couple of months. Most attention from the big labs has gone to video since that‘s where the money is. We have a page to track the history of it all here https://lumenfall.ai/arena/history

(Right now missing some models which I‘ll add today.)

item.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
item.description: 347 points, 247 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (openai.com)

→ HN comments  ·  347 points  ·  247 comments

Top #1 — darkamaul:

I would be curious to see the distribution of these vulns in the codebase:

- What subsystems are affected?

- What's the median age of the vulnerable code? Is more recent code stronger than old ones?

- What is the type of vulnerabilities found? Memory corruptions, logic bugs, race conditions, ...

This is an impressive result, but we need more info to understand how well this would translate to another codebase, and what lessons can be drawn from this experiment. Not every company has ~million dollards in tokens to spend.

↳ reply — bananaquant:

Good points. Unfortunately, they don't have the people nor the incentive to actually look into that.

Also, let's maybe not call the result impressive until we see what's under the hood.

↳↳ reply — fauigerzigerk:

>Unfortunately, they don't have the people nor the incentive to actually look into that.

These are relatively simple statistics. Some are even trivial. I don't see why it requires any people at all.

It wouldn't even have to be done by OpenAI. Given a list of vulnerabilities, it wouldn't be too hard for third parties to collect these statistics.

Top #2 — Plasmoid:

How did we get to the point where there are a thousand privilege escalation exploits in the kernel?

Is the kernel simply too complex to reason about? Is it an underlying flaw in the security model or language implementation?

Should we assume that all software is more compromised than the kernel?

↳ reply 1 — beala:

Many people seem to be making this about their pet issue, but "these systems are complex" and "the frontier labs have developed models that are superhuman at hacking" seems like a totally sufficient explanation.

I've been working with a LoRa chip called the LR2021. I plugged a dev board into my computer and told Claude to reverse engineer it. He dissected it with a speed and level of efficiency I couldn't believe. Within a few hours, Claude was writing custom patches for a completely opaque patch RAM area meant only for the manufacture. I wrote about it here: https://beala.substack.com/p/your-node-doesnt-need-a-microco...

↳↳ reply — Gigachad:

The stuff we have seen so far feels less like super human hacking skills and more human skills at superhuman scale.

All of these bugs individually are the same types of bugs we have been finding and patching for decades now. But we found a way to scale that far beyond what we had before.

↳ reply 2 — vbezhenar:

That's the drawback of monolithic Linux and tendency to put everything in kernel.

It is absolutely possible to have very minimal kernel with drivers and many other subsystems running with lowered privileges.

That would greatly reduce privilege escalation possibilities. Right now single vulnerability in any kernel subsystem gives you highest access to the system.

Imagine that some USB device driver runs as "nobody:nobody" process having access only to selected syscalls related to its functions. Even if it has vulnerability, you won't go anywhere from there.

Modularity and very granular access controls are the "secret" to secure system.

And the most privileged part of the kernel could be so small that it could be verified with advanced methods, basically proving its correctness.

Top #3 — dangelosaurus:

This is my team’s work. I’m happy to try to answer questions or take questions back to the team.

And we're hiring! https://openai.com/careers/search/?q=cyber

↳ reply 1 — amluto:

Do you have a list of the publicly discussed or fixed ones?

(As someone who used to handle nonpublic Linux kernel security reports and is still very interested in this stuff, I’d love to review a small sample of these reports to get a feel for what kinds of issues are being unearthed.)

Also, please don’t stop at LPEs and information disclosures. If you find cases where Linux can be convinced to misbehave or where the implemented semantics don’t make sense, these are good, too. I’ve found plenty of interesting kernel bugs, including some juicy LPEs, and almost none were memory safety errors :)

↳ reply 2 — BoppreH:

It's a bittersweet result, like finding asbestos in your house. I'd rather know than not, but I would much prefer not having it in the first place.

I understand this work was based on a dated snapshot. Will there be any continuous effort, scanning new PRs as they land, to prevent new weaknesses from being added?

item.title: Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor Part 3: Bad Update Improvements
item.description: 134 points, 12 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (icode4.coffee)

→ HN comments  ·  134 points  ·  12 comments

Top #1 — ElCapitanMarkla:

Perfectly timed post… I picked up a Corona 360 with 250GB HD yesterday for $50. Installed BadUpdate 1.3 last night and it all worked perfectly. The boy has been having a blast with it

↳↳↳ reply — tgsovlerkhgsel:

Which means that if the ad companies have consequences for letting through scams, new identities will face restrictions (e.g. identity verification, initial safety deposit, not being able to advertise on most surfaces) until they find a way to keep the scams out or die trying.

Of course, this will cost money, both because it will cost them legitimate customers that get caught up in the friction and because implementing the measures/reviews has costs, so they will only do it if forced. If they can just externalize the cost (in the form of scam victims getting hurt by scams) and/or can profit from the scams without sufficient downsides, they're going to do just that...

↳ reply 2 — 2OEH8eoCRo0:

Top #2 — beloch:

(You should too!) I won't consider changing this recommendation until Google and other ad servers start caring enough to filter out scam ads.

item.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
item.description: 1065 points, 342 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (layer3intel.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1065 points  ·  342 comments

Top #1 — btown:

The danger here, of course, is that while these compromised devices are currently being monetized in a relatively benign way (other than bandwidth costs to the user, which to be sure can be nontrivial)… it would be naive to assume that there isn't a Command and Control capability that can assign less benign tasking - or can be compromised to do so.

This also puts some of the troubling reports that politicians were bringing phones into SCIFs into context…

↳ reply 1 — mzajc:

> benign

On a server that used to get below 1k HTTP requests a day, I've had several cases of mass scraping from these botnets exceeding 100req/s. The web is getting harder and harder to use due to all the anti-bot mechanisms site operators had to put up.

How is DDOSing every site on the web benign?

↳↳ reply — nucleardog:

Relatively benign.

A compromised device inside the White House network could presumably be doing something _much_ worse than participating in a DDOS against random websites.

↳↳↳ reply — mcv:

And it's right there in the second line of the article:

> One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Surely a Russian company known for cyberattacks against the US having direct access to the White House network is far more serious than just DDOSing random websites. This is espionage at the highest level. (Again.)

↳ reply 2 — _alternator_:

I'll just note that "compromised" is perhaps too strong. These services often come from VPN plugins (eg Hola VPN) that lets users watch sports from different restricted geographic regions. There is a trade here that's in the TOs: you get someone else's IP address, they get yours.

↳ reply 3 — 50208:

Why wouldn't an adversary be using it to conceal command and control traffic?

Top #2 — dhosek:

They’re too polite to say it explicitly, but when they say:

> Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

There really aren’t very many candidates for who that person might be and it really seems like it would be someone who, I don’t know, maybe lives where the traffic is originating.

↳ reply 1 — dpark:

A lot of people work at the White House. Many of them doubtless work a night shift. The set of candidates here is actually quite large.

↳↳ reply — mrandish:

> A lot of people work at the White House.

I'm no expert but even I've read that "Works at the White House" is bigger than the executive residence and oval office, including the West Wing and the big office building that's directly connected to it by basement walkways. The National Security Council maintains 24-hour watch operations in the Situation Room (which is more a 'complex' than 'room'), while regional desk officers routinely work late evenings to overlap with morning business hours in Europe and Asia.

I asked Gemini if my recollection was correct and got: "The EOP network (managed by the EOP Office of Administration in coordination with Presidential Information Technology Community entities like the White House Communications Agency) operates as a single campus enterprise network. Its high-speed backbone links the West Wing, the EEOB, the East Wing, and nearby administrative facilities such as the New Executive Office Building (NEOB) on 17th Street."

So, definitely an issue that there's a device with some rogue malware installed but the total workforce across all shifts at the White House Complex is roughly between 2,500 and 4,000.

↳↳↳ reply — HaZeust:

"and the big office building that's directly connected to it by basement walkways"

I ask in good faith, but why didn't you just say the Treasury Building?

↳ reply 2 — ajcp:

Even at midnight I can't imagine there being less than 100 people working at the WH in various capacities. While it's probably not the duty/desk officers in the Situation Room/Security Council, there are plenty of maintenance staff that work at night. 5-midnight seems like it overlaps perfectly with a shift schedule.

Top #3 — bronco21016:

Gotta have your SuperBox set up to watch 24 hr cable news working late into the night.

↳ reply 1 — Tangurena2:

For those who don't know what this is, here's a decent podcast about it:

https://darknetdiaries.com/episode/172/

There's a transcript if you want to read, not listen. At the start, you'll be "hey! I gotta get me one!" and later you'll be like "burn it with fire!"

↳↳ reply — yard2010:

> I get a hit in my vulnerability log, like in the threat log on my Palo Alto firewall, and it’s for a SCADA vulnerability. ... A SCADA vulnerability. This makes no sense. SCADA is the control systems used in large-scale industrial settings. Think pumps, valves, conveyor belts, compressors, elevators, railway switches. This is where SCADA systems live. Why in the world is this box that’s here to deliver TV and movies attempting to trigger a SCADA exploit on D3ada55’ network? This is very concerning.

Such things are threats to humanity imho. They can get us back to the times we couldn't exploit the internet to run a society.

↳ reply 2 — JTbane:

I have seen these at mall kiosks advertising "free cable", and today I learned they are proxying from your home network.

→ HN comments  ·  149 points  ·  59 comments

Top #1 — WarOnPrivacy:

Buy for the low, low price of - nope. Not for you.

    $4,699/mo (monthly term) or $3,759/mo (annual term)

ref: https://cloud-gpus.com/qualcomm-ai-100-ultra/

↳ reply — fancyfredbot:

↳↳ reply — teruakohatu:

Top #2 — thway15269037:

↳ reply 1 — simlevesque:

According to their own website, they cost 1 cent.

↳↳ reply — thway15269037:

Yeah, I clicked that too. But knowing qualcomm they obviously cost an arm and a leg. Still interesting how much.

↳ reply 2 — dingdingdang:

Honestly, let me buy one, it's many times faster than the minipc I run local ai on so if the price is right I'm in.

Top #3 — zitterbewegung:

Sort of interesting design It has half a terabyte of SRAM on the accelerator with a 128 GB of RAM replacing HBM with SRAM but keeping regular RAM.

↳ reply — 2001zhaozhao:

half a gigabyte not terabyte lol

↳↳ reply — zrm:

Yeah, this thing is unusual. It resembles a consumer GPU but using normal DRAM with more channels, so then you get more RAM but less memory bandwidth than GDDR/HBM, which is the same thing Apple does. And the TDP is pretty attractive for what it is.

But what is that amount of SRAM for? It simultaneously seems like a lot, because SRAM is so expensive, but still not very much, because what can you fit in 0.5GB? Is there a specific workload that needs something that looks like this?

↳↳↳ reply — tromp:

0.5 GB of SRAM is exactly what the Cuckatoo32 [1] Proof-of-Work scheme needs for optimal solving efficiency. Solutions are 42-cycles in random bipartite graphs of 2^32 edges on 2^32 + 2^32 nodes, which can be found by repeatedly removing edges that have only one adjacent edge. Tracking which nodes have incident edges takes 2^32 (completely randomly accessed) bits which is exactly 0.5GB. Another 0.5 GB is needed to track alive edges but those can be accessed serially for which DRAM suffices.

[1] https://github.com/tromp/cuckoo

item.title: Insects don't swarm at LED lights
item.description: 264 points, 128 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (birdsoutsidemywindow.org)

→ HN comments  ·  264 points  ·  128 comments

Top #1 — tw04:

I have LED headlights and an LED light bar on my tractor and I can say with 100% confidence that bugs swarm both. To the point I have to wear glasses to keep them out of my eyes if I’m on it for more than about 30 seconds at night.

I’m guessing he’s confusing the dramatic drop in insect life overall with a change in behavior due to different lights.

↳ reply 1 — Izmaki:

I second this. When my home was infested by flies (I stopped counting at ~1000 over a 3 week period) they would always swarm and hang out by my grow lights (full spectrum LEDs) in my kitchen window. It was a great place for fly traps on the flip side.

It is quite possible that flies prefer one part of the light spectrum more than another part, but to say in the title that they don’t swarm at LEDs is misleading at best.

↳↳ reply — Freestyler_3:

Its possible grow lights emit a bit of uv.

↳↳↳ reply — joshspankit:

I would even say it’s very likely. Most Blue LEDs emit UV, and a lot of other-coloured LEDs are blue with a phosphor coating

↳ reply 2 — wopwops:

Yep, my Fenix headlamp and flashlights attract flying insects like crazy.

Top #2 — gopalv:

My pet theory is that the dimmable LEDs repel insects (when used as a grow light).

The thing that insects can see and we don't is the rapid flashing of a PWM power controller.

I wonder if these streetlights have power saving fade-ins as the nightfall approaches instead of clicking on at sunset.

Like - https://doi.org/10.1109/CSNT51715.2021.9509652

↳ reply 1 — winrid:

This. It likely depends on the driving technology. Some repell me too :P

Note you can make LEDs dim without PWM via constant current drivers, just less efficient as the duty cycle is 100%, they look much nicer though

↳↳ reply — nik282000:

PWM drivers should be banned, the quality of lighting is horrendous and it murders LEDs. You have an rms currernt that is in spec but the peak is way too high.

anecdote: I work in a factory, we have thousands of light fixtures. The older constant current LED fixtures have lasted a decade, the new PWM driven lights have had a ~1% failure rate.

↳ reply 2 — andai:

One of my favorite things I read growing up was a passage about what it's like to be a fly watching TV.

In those days TV's were big CRT boxes, illuminated by the electron beam which would race across the screen row by row.

A housefly's "refresh rate" on its eyeballs is much higher than that of a human, so the fly wouldn't see an image as we do, but would presumably find it quite relaxing watching the dot of light slowly move across the screen.

Top #3 — dylan604:

I love to shoot long exposure timelapse of the night sky. I set up a couple of LEDs dimmed as low as possible to light a bit of the foreground (over the course of the long exposure the low light adds up so it looks normal for those not familiar). Out of sheer laziness, I just placed them on either side of my tripod. The next day after processing the shot, it was pretty much ruined because of all of the bugs showing up as tracers in each frame.

So, no, not my experience at all.

↳ reply 1 — hinkley:

Bugs don’t just materialize out of the ether to swarm lights. Not to feed swallows. They are there and you will encounter them if the density is much more than zero.

There are bugs. You photographed bugs. Maybe more than you would have without lights at all, maybe about the same.

Also better lights don’t necessarily mean perfect lights. We do lots of things to reduce harm. Unfortunately sometimes we do them too much and conserve a significant fraction of the original harm by increasing demand.

↳↳ reply — andai:

>Not to feed swallows.

I often visit a place full of swallows and mosquitoes. The swallows eat mosquitoes, and the mosquitoes eat me. So when I get bit, I joke I'm feeding the birds.

↳↳↳ reply — hinkley:

The circle of life!

↳ reply 2 — edoceo:

Can we see that? Bet it looks cool.

item.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
item.description: 295 points, 108 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ricursive.com)

→ HN comments  ·  295 points  ·  108 comments

Top #1 — advael:

Category narrowing to this degree really has diluted the term "SOTA" quite a lot

You mean it's state of the art for this subset of benchmarks you're targeting? No? Well surely it's state of the art for models of a certain size category? Huh, what about models that are available for local inference? O, state of the art for open models of a certain size made in the US specifically. Uh. Neat!

↳ reply 1 — gpm:

Playing games like this also makes it very easy to accidentally say things that aren't true, like in the headline of the article...

> Introducing Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight Model

It's not "frontier", it's not "frontier" even in the category of open-weight models (though usually that phrasing would mean frontier over all, and also open weight)... it's only "frontier" in the small sub-category of US made open-weight models.

↳↳ reply — GuB-42:

It is technically frontier, if by "frontier" we mean the Pareto frontier.

Being at the Pareto frontier means that you can't get something better on one aspect without compromising on some other aspect. The trick is that it is easy to be at the Pareto frontier by having enough dimensions.

Here, we have 4: score, number of parameters, origin (US) and open-weight. You can get a better score or a lower number of parameters, but you have to compromise on at least one of the other aspects. That's a pretty weak frontier if you ask me.

↳↳↳ reply — derefr:

“Origin” isn’t part of the Pareto frontier because it’s not a quantitative dimension.

(You could say that “ability to be trusted by US government/military users” is quantifiable, but I would argue that by that metric, this model falls behind non-US-originated open-weight models that have more eyes on them!)

↳ reply 2 — msy:

It's like the Baseball World Series of Frontier models. It's SOTA in the same way Tesla are SOTA EVs - the best you're permitted to buy in the USA.

↳ reply 3 — yorwba:

AFAIK the currently biggest US open-weight model is Inkling, which they include in the comparison, so at least their claim is not limited to a size category. Still they score 0.42 percentage points higher than the second-best model on their chosen benchmark, so it's hardly a meaningful lead.

Top #2 — stewartpark:

It's great to see another competitive open weight model. Congratulations!

But as is, it's probably hard to become popular amongst hobbyists and local model enthusiasts like Qwen's 27B class models or MOE models because it's a 65B dense model and inference will be prohibitively slow on consumer grade hardware, and seems like the goal/mission of the company behind this model is to automate chip design.

So if I have to assume and connect the dots, this is for the companies who want to use AI in air-gapped environments for chip design so that they protect their IPs (not leaking to third party AI labs/hostile parties) and can afford lots of server grade inference hardware for a quick unlock with the big dense model.

Neat!

↳ reply 1 — deepsquirrelnet:

> it's a 65B dense model and inference will be prohibitively slow on consumer grade hardware

Times are changing and with MTP and DFLASH, dense models are back in style. For qwen 3.8 27b, you can get great token generation rates with MTP and for quality, it's much better than a MoE of comparable size.

↳↳ reply — stewartpark:

That helps, yes. But speculative decoding that requires a secondary/draft model means a trade off (smaller KV pool), so often times the only option left is MTP unless you have lots of VRAM. And as you already know, these options (MTP, DFlash, DSpark, etc) are also available for MoE models, too. If it's 3tk/s instead of 1tk/s, we can say it helps but not sure how many people would be excited about that. I'd be more excited about 150tk/s instead of 50tk/s!

↳ reply 2 — 59nadir:

Is it competitive overall or just competitive when compared to "U.S. Open-Weight models that are otherwise pretty decent at agentic coding"? The latter does not imply the former.

Top #3 — wmf:

Congratulations I guess but it's a pretty bad look to not even mention those other open weight models.

↳ reply 1 — karmakaze:

What's funnier is that after cherry picking models for comparison, they further cherry picked Inking for size comparison instead of better and smaller Beam 1.0

The bar chart also shows Nemotron 3 Ultra instead of smaller and better Nemotron 3.5 Super.

↳ reply 2 — tedivm:

We've always been at war with eurasia.

Seriously though, it's just easier to pretend that China doesn't exist when they're stomping us this badly.

item.title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
item.description: 193 points, 25 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (fireflyk64.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  193 points  ·  25 comments

Top #1 — daniel_rh:

Author here: in 2015, I was playing the classic Wing Commander in DOSBox and suddenly realized the game state fit in the 64k data segment.

Over ten years my brother and I went through a set of experiments (stop and go, turn, communicate) while probing the memory. We uncovered where the variables were, how to inject calls into the game functions, and how to sync the gamestate across the network, so we can fly the story missions together.

My favorite finding is that the camera lives in entity slot 0x3D, which is possibly a "3D" reference by the original developers.

You can play it at https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox in browser. If you own Wing Commander, drag in the installer since no game files are hosted. If you don't, the page will load the original DOS/3Dfx version of Vega Strike, before I open sourced it. I upscaled and redid DOS Vega Strike art using AI, but it now has multiplayer and a similar feel.

I'll be in the lobby for the next few hours if anyone wants to fly together.

Disclosure: I also used AI for the final step to help compile for the browser and port our TCP networking stack to WebRTC with voice and solve a few lingering bugs.

↳ reply 1 — cadr:

I don't know if I'm more impressed with the result, or that you kept coming back to it for a decade. Super cool!

↳ reply 2 — frikk:

helllllll yeah. i think it's awesome when domain experts and clever humans use AI to automate the implementation after they've designed the path through the forest. Nice work.

Top #2 — herodoturtle:

These are the sorts of posts I come to Hacker News for.

What a brilliantly fun project to share with the world. Thank you to the authors.

Top #3 — Tepix:

Neat! You're using the data channel for voice? why not the rtc stream?

↳ reply — daniel_rh:

Thanks for the feedback! I'll have a look. I do worry about congestion coupling since it would mean a bursty voice stream could affect game packets. Keeping it on a different stream allows game data priority over voice.

I did befriend a murderer once.

item.title: Education shouldn't be held for ransom
item.description: 126 points, 83 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.kagi.com)

→ HN comments  ·  126 points  ·  83 comments

Top #1 — SeanAnderson:

I haven't felt as concerned about this news article as others.

IME, schools really don't have a good grasp on what AI means in relationship to them and what policies would result in better outcomes.

I work in the ed tech parent-teacher communication space. We offer automatic translations of communication to other languages via Google Translate. Google Translate uses AI. Schools come to us and tell us we need to disable all our AI features. We do. Then they freak out asking where their feature went. We explain. They say they don't want to lose translations they just don't want to deal with "AI stuff"

It's not clear to me if this stance from Google is a new thing. Did they recently add AI to search and are trying to use bundling behaviors to incept AI into areas it wouldn't be? Or did policy recently become rabid against the use of AI without fully appreciating the ask and ramifications? Both?

↳ reply 1 — SamBam:

Schools want to control whether Gemini and other generative AI is available to students.

I'm a middle school science teacher. We've already moved much of our work to paper because of this issue, but there is so much good science that should be done using computer simulations and other tools. So I do have computers out for some lessons.

So now, on a lesson where a computer is out, a student can instantly type in a question on the Google search bar, get an AI answer, and write it down with zero thoughts traveling through their heads.

Yes, redesign the lesson. Yes, if computers are out don't ask questions that an AI can answer. But you know what? Instead of needing to cut out everything that makes a lesson a productive struggle for kids, it would be great just to not have Gemini cheat for them.

↳↳ reply — mikeleeorg:

> Schools want to control whether Gemini and other generative AI is available to students.

I really wish more articles and social media posts point this out, but a lot of writers either don't know this distinction or are going with a more "clickbaity" angle on purpose.

↳ reply 2 — stevemk14ebr:

This is basically pedantry, they want generative AI and AI search off. If anyone is confused then you should be asking more questions to understand the desires.

↳ reply 3 — paxy:

Yeah it's pretty likely that schools are adding strict no AI clauses in their Google Workplace contracts and Google's lawyers are including search in that definition just to be safe. If they then want to enable it manually, sure.

Top #2 — danielciocirlan:

Education is going to be left in tatters after AIs creep into every facet of (tech-enabled) life.

Big tech doesn’t care about teaching people to think. All the money is in the capture of attention, and AI will only make everything 100x more convenient and a no-brainer (quite literally) to pick the hard way of thought and effort for just about anything… as long as the user is caught. Education has fundamentally the opposite goal.

↳ reply — beezlebroxxxxxx:

> Education is going to be left in tatters

Public, free education will. People who can afford it are sending their kids to schools with very strict technology policies, stricter than what is possible in many public schools nowadays (for a number of reasons).

It's very much a "for the masses" mindset with the people who gain from this kind of relationship between technology and public schools.

↳↳ reply — JuniperMesos:

Public free education is already in tatters in many neighborhoods and has been for many decades. People already pay a lot of money to live in a neighborhood with expensive housing prices in order to price out from living there people whose children would make the local public school worse (by e.g. getting into physical fights). People sometimes pay for a private school to avoid this because it is cheaper than a house in a neighborhood with people whose children make good students to spend time in close physical proximity with.

Top #3 — ahmedfromtunis:

It's ironic that Kagi uses confusion (as to not say deception) to market itself as the more ethical brand.

Google clarified that admins can turn on and off each of the options independently, including search without AI.

I don't like to defend trillion-dollar companies in my free time, but what Kagi is trying to do with this piece is not good.

↳ reply — kelgan:
